 Why trust EnergySage? 
 EnergySage Power outages don't have to mean scrambling for candles or worrying about spoiled food. With the right backup power solution, you can maintain your normal routines even when the grid goes down. Battery backup systems offer a clean, quiet alternative to noisy generators, providing reliable power when you need it most. 
 While many homeowners opt for partial backup systems that power essential appliances, whole-home battery backup takes energy independence to the next level. These robust systems can keep your entire house running during extended outages, from your HVAC system to your home office setup. 
 We'll cover what you need to know about whole-home battery backup—what it is, whether it's right for your home, and which systems offer the best performance and value in 2026.

 What is whole-home battery backup? 
 Whole-home battery backup systems store enough electricity to power your entire house during an outage, maintaining normal energy consumption levels without any lifestyle changes. Unlike partial backup systems that only support essential loads like refrigerators, lights, and internet, whole-home setups keep every outlet, appliance, and system in your home operational. 
 The key difference lies in capacity and power output. Whole-home systems typically require 30 kilowatt-hours (kWh) or more of battery storage capacity—roughly equivalent to an average home's daily electricity consumption. A system this large comes with a higher price tag, often costing three times as much as a partial backup system.

 The batteries used in both systems are identical—whole-home backup simply requires more of them. Think of it like generators : You can choose a small portable unit for essential needs or a standby generator for your entire house. The difference is that battery backup systems rely on clean, stored electricity rather than expensive fuel. 
 Do you need whole-home or partial-home battery backup? 
 For most American homes, partial battery backup systems make more sense financially and practically. Extended power outages are relatively infrequent in most parts of the country, making the extra investment in whole-home capacity unnecessary for typical use cases. 
 However, whole-home battery backup may be worth considering if you: 
 Live in an area with frequent or prolonged outages 
 Work from home and need uninterrupted power for equipment 
 Have medical devices that require consistent electricity 
 Want complete energy independence during grid disruptions 
 Have a large home with high electricity consumption 
 The decision often depends on your risk tolerance, budget, and how much inconvenience you're willing to accept during outages.

 The Tesla Powerwall 3 earns the top spot with a well-rounded set of specs. It offers one of the higher continuous power ratings on this list at 11.5 kW, along with a strong power-to-energy ratio, making it capable of running multiple appliances at once without issue. 
 It’s also one of the most intelligent batteries. It automatically detects outages, switches to backup power instantly, and can manage where your home gets its energy around time-of-use rates to maximize savings. Its 97.5% roundtrip efficiency and an unlimited-cycle warranty mean you get more usable power from every charge; it's built for both performance and long-term use. 
 One of the highlight features of the Powerwall 3 is the built-in hybrid inverter that supports both AC and DC coupling, providing plenty of flexibility. That said, you’ll get the most out of it when DC-coupled within Tesla’s ecosystem. If your system relies on microinverters or panel-level optimization, you won’t realize the full potential of the battery. 
 2. FranklinWH aPower 2: Best for retrofits 
 Price: $1,177/kWh 
 Capacity per unit: 15 kWh 
 If you already have solar, the FranklinWH aPower 2 is one of the easiest batteries to add to your home. It’s AC-coupled, so it works with almost any existing inverter setup—no major rewiring or replacement needed. 
 Like the Powerwall, the aPower2 is also an intelligent system. It can automatically handle outages and shift usage around time-of-use rates , so you don’t have to think about it day to day. Each unit gives you 15 kWh of usable capacity, 10 kW of continuous power, and a standout 15 kW peak output—which is especially useful for starting heavy loads like air conditioners or pumps. 
 The 15-year warranty is another major plus and among the longest on this list. 
 The tradeoffs are efficiency and cost. At 90% roundtrip efficiency, it lags behind most competitors on our list. It’s also not the cheapest option at $1,177/kWh—but the higher per-unit capacity means you typically need fewer batteries to reach whole-home coverage, which helps offset the higher price in real system sizing. 
 3. Renon Power Xtreme LV: Best power and price 
 Price: $882/kWh 
 Capacity per unit: 10.24 kWh (2 modules) 
 The Renon Xtreme LV is the value play on this list. At $882/kWh, it’s the most affordable option and the highest power output on our list—15.4 kW continuous and peak power (for the 20.48 configuration and up). 
 The downside is that Renon is still a newer brand. Specs are strong, but the installer network and long-term track record aren’t as established, so availability and support can take a little more effort to sort out. 
 4. EcoFlow Ocean Pro Solar Battery System: Best warranty 
 Price: $1,459/kWh 
 Capacity per unit: 10 kWh  
 The EcoFlow Ocean Pro stands out mostly for its warranty: 6,000 cycles and a 15-year term with a 70% end-of-warranty capacity, putting it at the top of the category for long-term coverage. It’s scalable and includes robust app-based monitoring, making it easy to track usage and backup status in real time. 
 But the tradeoffs are pretty clear. At 87% efficiency and $1,459/kWh, it’s the least efficient and most expensive option on the list.  
 5. EG4 WallMount All-Weather 280Ah: Best efficiency 
 Price: $1,163/kWh 
 Capacity per unit: 14.3 kWh  
 The EG4 WallMount is about as efficient as it gets at 99% roundtrip. The 8,000-cycle warranty is also a big deal, signaling that this is built to be used regularly, not just sit there for emergency backup. It’s built with a weather-rated enclosure to handle heat, moisture, and dust, so you’re not forced to give up garage or indoor space to install it.  
 Where it falls short is in intelligence. Unlike Tesla or FranklinWH, the EG4 doesn’t really manage energy on its own. Much of its “smartness” depends on the inverter and how the installer configures the system. So, while extremely efficient, it’s not the kind of system you can “set and forget” like the more advanced smart batteries.

 How to compare whole-home backup batteries 
 When evaluating different battery systems for whole-home backup, several key factors determine which option best fits your needs and budget. 
 Battery capacity and scalability 
 Usable capacity , measured in kWh, indicates how much electricity a battery can store and deliver to your home. For whole-home backup, you'll need a system with enough capacity to power your home for a full day—typically around 30 kWh for the average American household. 
 Some manufacturers design batteries with larger individual capacities, while others offer modular systems that let you stack multiple smaller units. Modular designs generally provide better scalability, allowing you to add capacity incrementally rather than replacing your entire system as your needs change. 
 Consider your future electricity needs when choosing a system. If you plan to add an electric vehicle, heat pump, or other high-consumption appliances, scalable systems offer more flexibility for expansion. 
 Battery chemistry 
 Battery chemistry determines how electricity is stored and affects the safety, stability, and lifespan of your system. Most home batteries use lithium-ion chemistry in one of three categories: 
 Lithium Iron Phosphate (LFP): Safe, stable, and relatively affordable. Most whole-home backup batteries use this chemistry. 
 Lithium Nickel Manganese Cobalt Oxide (NMC): Higher power density but less stable than LFP batteries. 
 Lithium Titanium Oxide (LTO): Highest quality and longest lifespan, but also the most expensive and least power-dense. 
 For whole-home backup applications, LFP batteries often provide the best balance of safety, performance, and cost-effectiveness. 
 Battery power output 
 Power output , measured in kilowatts (kW), determines how many appliances your battery can operate simultaneously. Two metrics matter for whole-home backup: 
 Peak power indicates the maximum power your battery can supply for short periods to start high-demand appliances like HVAC systems, well pumps, or electric dryers. 
 Continuous power refers to the sustained power output your battery can maintain over extended periods. For whole-home backup, you need sufficient continuous power to run multiple appliances simultaneously without exceeding the system's limits. 
 Battery configuration & efficiency 
 The coupling method affects how your battery integrates with your solar panels and home electrical system: 
 AC-coupled batteries convert electricity three times during storage and delivery, resulting in slightly lower efficiency. However, they're easier to install with existing solar systems and offer more flexibility for system design. 
 DC-coupled batteries convert electricity only once, maximizing efficiency but potentially limiting compatibility with certain solar inverter configurations. 
 Roundtrip efficiency measures how much stored electricity you can actually use. Higher efficiency means less energy loss during the storage process, maximizing the value of your battery investment. 
 Warranty protection 
 Battery warranties protect your significant investment by guaranteeing performance over time. When comparing warranties, examine these key aspects: 
 Warranty duration: Most batteries offer 10-year warranties, though some extend to 15 years or more. 
 End-of-warranty capacity: Batteries gradually lose capacity over time. Good warranties guarantee your battery will retain 70% or more of its original capacity by the end of the warranty period. 
 Throughput or cycle limitations: Some warranties limit how much electricity you can store over the warranty period or how many charge-discharge cycles you can complete. 
 Price considerations 
 Whole-home battery backup represents a substantial investment, typically costing roughly $34,000 or more before any available incentives. While the upfront cost is significant, consider the long-term value of energy independence and protection from power outages. 
 Factors affecting total cost include: 
 Battery capacity and number of units required 
 Installation complexity and electrical upgrades 
 Permitting and interconnection fees 
 Additional equipment like monitoring systems 
 Solar plus storage systems enhance your home’s resiliency 
 Battery backup systems provide crucial protection against power disruptions, but pairing them with solar panels creates true energy independence. This combination, known as solar-plus-storage, offers renewable resiliency that keeps your home powered even during extended grid outages. 
 Without battery backup, grid-connected solar systems shut down during outages for safety reasons—even if your panels generate enough electricity to power your entire home. Adding battery storage allows you to harness your solar production during outages while maintaining backup power for nighttime or cloudy conditions.

 Bill savings (time-of-use shifting). The battery stores your midday solar and runs your home in the late afternoon and evening, when utility rates are highest. Under California's current net-billing rules (NEM 3.0), this is where most of a battery's financial value comes from. Why NEM 3.0 changed the math .
 Self-consumption. Where your utility pays little or nothing for the solar you send back, a battery soaks up the extra and uses it later.
 Backup power. Without a battery (or a special "sunlight backup" setup), solar panels shut off during a grid outage for line-worker safety. A battery keeps essentials, or the whole house, running.

 Battery features, explained
 AC-coupled vs DC-coupled
 Solar panels make DC power, batteries store DC, and your home runs on AC. Each conversion loses a little energy. DC-coupled batteries store solar power directly and convert once, so they're a bit more efficient. AC-coupled batteries convert more often but are usually easier to add to an existing system.
 Round-trip efficiency
 How much of the energy you put in, you get back out. Most home batteries land around 89–90%. If your battery cycles every day for bill savings, a few points add up over the years.
 Usable capacity
 How much energy you can actually draw, in kWh. This is the number to compare, not the "nameplate" size.
 Continuous vs peak power
 Continuous power is what the battery can supply for hours, and it decides how much of your home runs in an outage. Peak power covers short surges, like an AC compressor starting.
 Backup vs consumption-only
 Backup hardware and wiring are expensive. Consumption-only batteries skip them and just store solar for later, for less: about 15–40% less on our marketplace, depending on the model. A no-backup Enphase IQ 5P, for example, is ~$6,125 versus ~$10,650 for the backup version. If outages aren't a concern where you live, it's the cheapest way to add battery savings. What is a consumption-only battery? 
 Battery chemistry

 Warranty
 Battery warranties typically guarantee about 70% of original capacity after 10–15 years or a set amount of use, whichever comes first. Read the throughput limit, not just the years.

 If you buy your battery (cash or loan), there's no federal tax credit in 2026. The homeowner credit ended at the end of 2025. The way to still capture that value is a Prepaid TPO (a prepaid lease): a partner owns the system for the first five years, claims the business credit, and passes it to you as an upfront discount on your price. You own it after year five. How the Prepaid TPO works 
 Some utilities and states also offer battery rebates, such as California's SGIP program when funding is open. Your installer should check what applies at your address.
 How to choose the right battery for you
 Start with your goal. Bill savings points to smaller or consumption-only batteries. Whole-home backup points to larger ones with high continuous power.
 Match the system. Enphase batteries fit best with Enphase microinverters; the Powerwall 3 replaces the solar inverter on a new system; FranklinWH works with almost anything.
 Compare price per usable kWh , not sticker price.
 Check the installer's battery track record. Our review data says that's where most battery projects go wrong. Start with the California installer rankings .

 Solar battery FAQs
 What is the best solar battery in 2026?
 Our top pick overall is the Tesla Powerwall 3, for its capacity, power, built-in inverter, and price per kWh. The Enphase IQ Battery 5P is the best fit for bill savings on a budget, and the FranklinWH aPower 2 is our pick for whole-home backup.
 How much does a Tesla Powerwall 3 cost installed?
 On the Solar.com marketplace, the median is about $15,000 when installed with a new solar system (Sept 2026), before rebates. Most installers fall between about $13,950 and $16,200.
 Is a solar battery worth it?
 It depends on your utility rates and your goals. Where evening rates are high or your utility pays little for exported solar, as in California under NEM 3.0, a battery often pays for itself through bill savings. In areas with frequent outages, the backup value can matter more than the payback math.
 Can I get a tax credit for a solar battery?
 Not if you buy it. The federal homeowner credit ended at the end of 2025. Through a Prepaid TPO, the credit value still reaches you as an upfront discount.
 How long do solar batteries last?
 Most carry 10–15 year warranties guaranteeing about 70% of original capacity. Many will run longer. Check the warranty's throughput limit as well as its length.
 What's the difference between lithium-ion and lead-acid batteries?
 Lithium batteries are lighter, more efficient, and last much longer, which is why nearly every modern home battery uses them. Lead-acid costs less up front but wears out faster and needs maintenance.

 Best Home Battery Backup 2026: 8 Systems Compared
 This article contains affiliate links: if you buy through them we may earn a commission, at no extra cost to you. Read our affiliate disclosure . 
 It’s the third outage this year. Last time you lost a freezer full of food and spent two nights listening to a neighbor’s generator through the bedroom wall. This time you want something that just works: the lights stay on, the sump pump keeps running, nobody goes out in the rain with a gas can. That’s what a home battery backup does, and in 2026 there are two very different ways to get one.
 The best home battery backup for most homes is the Tesla Powerwall 3: 13.5 kWh, up to 11.5 kW and a built-in solar inverter, installed by Tesla or a certified installer. For a lower starting price you can install in stages, the EcoFlow DELTA Pro Ultra delivers 7.2 kW at 120/240 V and grows to 90 kWh with an electrician-installed Smart Home Panel 2.
 Below: eight systems, four installer-only and four plug-in kits, with their real specs, warranties, prices where the maker publishes them, and how long each lasts in an outage. We researched and compared them from maker spec sheets, warranties and published pricing data; we did not test them.
 Prices change often. The prices below are what we saw at the maker or a major retailer in October 2026; check the current price before you buy. Installer systems have no public price, so get two or three quotes.

 Installer system or plug-in kit?
 Installer systems (Tesla, FranklinWH, Enphase, Generac) are designed, permitted and installed by the maker or its certified installers, fixed to a wall or pad and usually tied to solar. One company handles everything; EnergySage’s 2026 average is about $15,647 installed for 13.5 kWh, before incentives.
 Plug-in kits (EcoFlow, Anker SOLIX, BLUETTI, Jackery) are batteries you buy and can use right away with extension cords. For automatic backup of house circuits, a licensed electrician installs the maker’s panel, dock or a transfer switch. They cost less up front, grow over time and move with you.
 The best home battery backup systems
 1. Tesla Powerwall 3: best overall
 Powerwall 3 stores 13.5 kWh and delivers up to 11.5 kW continuously (installers can set it to 5.8, 7.6, 10 or 11.5 kW), with 185 A of locked-rotor start current for motors like a central AC compressor or well pump. Tesla built a solar inverter into it, rated for up to 20 kW of panels, and lists 89% solar-to-battery-to-home efficiency. You can add up to three Powerwall 3 Expansion units and run up to four Powerwall 3 units, seven in all. It weighs 291 lb installed. Tesla’s warranty is 10 years with 70% capacity retained, with unlimited cycles for solar self-use and backup.
 Good: lots of power for one unit, so one Powerwall can often cover whole-home backup; solar inverter included; sold by Tesla and certified installers.
 Watch out: 10-year warranty is shorter than Enphase’s or FranklinWH’s 15; Tesla publishes no list price; Tesla’s datasheet doesn’t name the battery chemistry; warranty is shorter if the system is kept offline.
 Best for: homes adding solar and a battery together, or anyone who wants one strong unit on the wall.
 See it at Tesla 
 2. FranklinWH aPower 2: most energy per unit
 The aPower 2 packs 15 kWh of LFP (lithium iron phosphate) battery with 10 kW continuous output, and short bursts of 15 kW for 10 seconds or 25 kW for one second. It works through FranklinWH’s aGate, which manages the switchover, and up to 15 units can connect to one aGate for 225 kWh. FranklinWH says a single aPower 2 can power an entire home, including A/C, and that it stores energy from solar, the grid, a generator or an EV. The warranty runs 15 years or 60 MWh of throughput, with at least 70% capacity retained.
 Good: most kWh per unit here; strong surge for motor loads; LFP chemistry; works with or without solar and with a generator.
 Watch out: needs the aGate on top of the battery; check that a certified FranklinWH installer serves your area; no public price.
 Best for: larger homes, homes without solar, and anyone who wants battery and generator in one system.
 See it at FranklinWH 
 3. Enphase IQ Battery 10C: best for Enphase solar homes
 The IQ Battery 10C holds 10.0 kWh of LFP battery and four built-in microinverters with a 7.08 kVA continuous rating, 56 A of peak current for three seconds and up to 90 A of locked-rotor start. It’s passively cooled (no fans), outdoor-rated (NEMA 3R) and under 33 dBA at one meter, and Enphase lists a charging range of –4°F to 122°F. It’s compatible with Enphase IQ and M Series microinverters, and you stack units for more storage. For smaller needs, the IQ Battery 5P stores 5.0 kWh with 3.84 kVA. Both carry Enphase’s warranty of 15 years or 6,000 cycles, to 60% capacity.
 Good: long warranty; nearly silent; field-replaceable components; evaluated to UL 9540A.
 Watch out: less power per unit than Powerwall 3, so whole-home backup with big motors may need two or more; 317 lb installed; best fit with Enphase solar.
 Best for: homes that already have, or are buying, Enphase microinverter solar.
 See it at Enphase 
 4. Generac PWRcell 2: best with a standby generator
 PWRcell 2 is built from 3 kWh modules: one cabinet holds 9, 12, 15 or 18 kWh, and two cabinets on one inverter reach 36 kWh. Continuous power grows with size, from 5.2 kW to 10.5 kW in one cabinet and 11.5 kW with two. It’s AC-coupled, works with Generac PWRmicro or Enphase IQ8 solar, and Generac says it supports whole-home backup up to 200 A service. The standout feature: it can integrate a Generac standby generator up to 28 kW, so the battery covers short outages silently and the generator takes over in long ones. Battery modules carry 10 years or 7.56 MWh; the inverter and cabinet 10 years.
 Good: size it in 3 kWh steps; battery-plus-generator in one system; sold through Generac installers.
 Watch out: 88% round-trip efficiency (a little lower than Enphase or FranklinWH); the spec sheet doesn’t name the chemistry; small cabinets have modest power.
 Best for: homes that have or want a Generac standby generator.
 See it at Generac 
 5. EcoFlow DELTA Pro Ultra: best plug-in whole-home kit
 The DELTA Pro Ultra is an inverter (7.2 kW continuous, 10.8 kW peak, 120/240 V) that stacks on 6.144 kWh LFP batteries. One inverter takes up to five batteries for 30 kWh; three inverters with the Smart Home Panel 2 reach 90 kWh and 21.6 kW. It accepts up to 5,600 W of solar, lists a backup switchover under 20 ms (0 ms on some outlets in online UPS mode), and carries UL 9540 and UL 1973 listings. EcoFlow rates it for 3,500 cycles to 80% and gives a five-year warranty. The Smart Home Panel 2 (12 circuits, about $1,599) connects it to your house; EcoFlow says the panel requires installation before use.
 Good: about $4,199 for inverter and one battery, or $5,599 with the panel (EcoFlow, October 2026); 240 V for well pumps; huge expansion.
 Watch out: heavy (inverter 70 lb, each battery 111.8 lb) and floor-standing, so plan the space; five-year warranty is short next to installer systems.
 Best for: homeowners who want whole-home-class backup now and more batteries later.
 Check the EcoFlow DELTA Pro Ultra price on Amazon 
 6. Anker SOLIX E10: best outdoor plug-in kit
 The E10 power module puts out 7.68 kW at 120/240 V, and with two or more B6000 batteries (6.144 kWh each) it can run at 10 kW for up to 90 minutes, with a start current Anker rates as equivalent to 155 A LRA. One module takes up to five batteries (about 30 kWh), and three E10 systems reach 90 kWh and 22.8 kW. It’s rated NEMA 4 (IP66) for outdoor installation, takes 9 kW of solar, and switches over in 20 ms or less. Anker rates the batteries for 4,000 cycles to 80%. An electrician installs the Smart Inlet Box or Power Dock; after that, Anker says you can add batteries yourself.
 Good: outdoor-rated, so it doesn’t take up a room; highest solar input of the plug-in kits; about $3,999 with one battery, $5,799 with Power Dock (Anker, October 2026).
 Watch out: the E10 carries a five-year warranty; Anker’s E10 page doesn’t name the battery chemistry; newer product with a shorter track record.
 Best for: homeowners who want an installer-style outdoor battery at a plug-in-kit price.
 Check the Anker SOLIX E10 price on Amazon 
 7. BLUETTI Apex 300: best budget expandable
 The Apex 300 starts at 2,764.8 Wh of LiFePO4 battery and 3,840 W of output, with 7,680 W of what BLUETTI calls “Lifting Power.” BLUETTI says it delivers 120 V and 240 V at the same time, switches in 0 ms as a UPS, and is rated for 6,000+ cycles to 80%. It takes up to 4,000 W of solar. The ceiling is high: three units with 18 B300K batteries reach 58 kWh and 11.52 kW. House circuits connect through BLUETTI’s Home Integration Kit or a transfer switch installed by an electrician.
 Good: about $1,499 (BLUETTI, October 2026); long cycle rating; grows a little at a time.
 Watch out: one unit is under 3 kWh, so plan on hours, not days, without more batteries; warranty length wasn’t stated on the page we read.
 Best for: starting small on a budget, with a path to a large system.
 Check the BLUETTI Apex 300 price on Amazon 
 8. Jackery HomePower 3000: best for essential circuits
 The HomePower 3000 is a 3,072 Wh LiFePO4 unit with 3,600 W of output (7,200 W peak), four 20 A outlets and one 30 A outlet, at 59.5 lb. It recharges from the wall in about 2.2 hours, takes 1,000 W of solar, and lists a 20 ms UPS switchover. It isn’t expandable. Jackery pairs it with a manual transfer switch for up to six circuits, installed by an electrician. Warranty: three years, plus two more when bought at jackery.com; Jackery rates it for 4,000 cycles to 70%.
 Good: lowest price here at about $1,349 (Jackery, October 2026); light enough to move; simple.
 Watch out: not expandable; no 240 V output listed in the specs we read; Jackery says its power stations are not recommended for medical or life-support equipment.
 Best for: fridge, lights, Wi-Fi and a furnace blower through short outages.
 Check the Jackery HomePower 3000 price on Amazon 
 How to choose a home battery backup
 Decide: essentials or whole home. A fridge, freezer, Wi-Fi, LED lights, a laptop and a sump pump running an hour add up to about 3.5 kWh a day in our example (ENERGY STAR median fridge and freezer, Zoeller pump specs). The average US home uses about 29.6 kWh a day (EIA, 2022).
 Size the kWh. Days of backup ≈ usable kWh ÷ daily kWh. Installer systems publish usable kWh; for plug-in kits we count 85% of the rating. A Powerwall 3 covers those essentials for about 3.8 days but an average whole home for about 11 hours; one 6.144 kWh EcoFlow or Anker battery covers essentials for about 1.5 days. These are our estimates, before any solar recharge.
 Check the kW and start current. Add up what runs at once. Motors need a start burst: compare the motor’s locked-rotor amps with the battery’s rating (185 A for Powerwall 3 and aPower 2, up to 90 A for one IQ Battery 10C).
 Need 240 V? Well pumps, central AC and some furnaces do. All four installer systems and the DELTA Pro Ultra, E10 and Apex 300 handle it; the specs we read for the HomePower 3000 list no 240 V output.
 Plan the recharge. With solar, a battery only has to cover the nights. Without it, a long outage is a fixed tank; pairing with a generator (Generac PWRcell 2, FranklinWH) is the other way to stretch it.
 Read the warranty, not just the years. Look for the capacity promised at the end and any energy-throughput cap.
 Every connection to house wiring, whether an installer system, a maker panel or a transfer switch, is installed by a licensed electrician, with a permit where required. Never backfeed a house by plugging a battery or generator into a wall outlet; FEMA and CPSC warn it can electrocute utility workers. There’s no federal tax credit for home batteries installed in 2026 (25D ended after December 31, 2025), but some states and utilities pay rebates or run battery programs: check DSIRE and your utility.
 Keep exploring
 Our home battery backup guide explains how these systems work and how to size one. Check the home battery backup cost , weigh a home battery vs a generator , or compare Tesla Powerwall vs Enphase . On a tighter budget, the best portable power station for home backup needs no installation, and our home generators guide covers the gas option. Learn how batteries pair with solar energy , and browse the whole home battery backup section.
 Home battery backup questions
 What is the best home battery backup in 2026?
 For most homes, the Tesla Powerwall 3: 13.5 kWh and up to 11.5 kW in one installed unit, with a solar inverter built in. For the most storage per unit, the 15 kWh FranklinWH aPower 2. If you’d rather buy a system and add batteries over time, the EcoFlow DELTA Pro Ultra with Smart Home Panel 2.
 How many home batteries do I need?
 For essentials (about 3.5 kWh a day in our example), one 10 to 15 kWh battery covers roughly three to four days. To run an average home (about 29.6 kWh a day, EIA) for a full day, plan on two or more large batteries, or solar to recharge. Your installer should size it from your own bills and the motors you need to start.
 How much does a home battery backup cost?
 EnergySage’s 2026 average is about $1,159 per kWh installed, or $15,647 for a 13.5 kWh system, before incentives. Plug-in kits start lower, from about $1,349 (Jackery HomePower 3000) to about $5,599 for an EcoFlow DELTA Pro Ultra with Smart Home Panel 2, plus the electrician’s work. Get two or three quotes.
 Can I buy a Tesla Powerwall on Amazon?
 No. Tesla Powerwall, Enphase IQ Battery, FranklinWH and Generac PWRcell are sold and installed through the maker or certified installers, because they’re wired into your main panel and need a permit. The plug-in kits from EcoFlow, Anker SOLIX, BLUETTI and Jackery are sold online, but their home panels still need an electrician.
 Do home batteries work without solar?
 Yes. They charge from the grid and wait for an outage. Without solar, though, the battery can’t refill until the grid returns, so size it for the outage length you expect. See the best home battery backup without solar .
 Written by SolutionEnergy Team

 Home Battery Backup: How It Works, What It Costs and the Best Systems
 This article contains affiliate links: if you buy through them we may earn a commission, at no extra cost to you. Read our affiliate disclosure . 
 The storm takes the power out a little after midnight. In most houses on the street, that means silence, a warm fridge by morning and a scramble for flashlights. In one house, the lights blink for a moment and stay on. The fridge keeps humming, the Wi-Fi never drops and the sump pump in the basement keeps doing its job. Nobody has to go outside to start anything, and there’s no engine noise and no exhaust. That house has a home battery backup .
 In short: a home battery backup is a large battery wired into your home’s electrical panel that switches on automatically when the grid fails. A typical installed system stores 10 to 15 kWh, enough for essentials (fridge, lights, Wi-Fi, a sump pump) for two to four days, but only about half a day for an average whole home. EnergySage puts the average installed cost at about $1,159 per kWh in 2026.
 This page starts our Home Battery Backup section: how home batteries work with and without solar, whole-home vs essentials, sizing, outage runtimes, 2026 costs, how they compare with generators and power stations, and our picks.
 Home battery backup at a glance
 What it is: a battery, an inverter and a switching device (gateway, transfer switch or smart panel) that keeps your house circuits powered when the grid goes down.
 Two kinds: installer systems that are bolted to a wall and wired in (Tesla Powerwall 3, Enphase IQ Battery, FranklinWH aPower 2, Generac PWRcell 2), and plug-in, expandable kits you buy yourself and connect through an electrician-installed panel (EcoFlow DELTA Pro Ultra, Anker SOLIX E10, BLUETTI Apex 300, Jackery HomePower 3000).
 Two numbers matter: kWh (how much energy it stores, which decides how long it lasts) and kW (how much it can deliver at once, which decides what it can run).
 Solar is optional: a battery can charge from the grid and wait for an outage. Solar lets it refill during a long one.
 Silent and fuel-free: no exhaust, no carbon monoxide, no gasoline to store.
 Cost: about $15,647 installed for a 13.5 kWh system on average (EnergySage, 2026 quotes); plug-in kits start around $1,349 for 3 kWh plus an electrician’s bill.
 No federal tax credit in 2026: the 25D residential clean energy credit ended for systems installed after December 31, 2025. State and utility programs remain in some places.
 What is a home battery backup and how does it work?
 Every home battery system has three jobs: store energy, turn it into the 120/240 V AC power your house uses, and separate your home from the grid the instant the grid fails. That last part matters. When the power goes out, the system opens a switch so your battery isn’t feeding the utility lines (that would endanger line workers), then powers your circuits on its own. Tesla calls this box a Backup Gateway, Enphase an IQ System Controller, FranklinWH an aGate, Generac a Smart Disconnect Switch, and EcoFlow and Anker a smart home panel or power dock.
 In normal times the battery sits charged. Many systems also do day-to-day work: storing solar power for the evening, or charging when electricity is cheap and discharging when it’s expensive on a time-of-use rate. When an outage hits, the switchover takes milliseconds; makers quote 20 ms or less for the EcoFlow Smart Home Panel 2 and the Anker SOLIX E10. Most people notice a blink, if anything.
 Installer systems vs plug-in expandable kits
 Installer systems are sold and installed through the maker or its certified installers. You get a quote, a permit, a fixed wall or ground mount (often outdoors) and one warranty for the whole job. They store 5 to 15 kWh per unit and stack for more. You can’t buy them on Amazon.
 Plug-in expandable kits are big power stations on wheels with add-on batteries. You can buy and use one tomorrow with extension cords. To power house circuits automatically, you add the maker’s panel or dock, and that part must be installed by a licensed electrician. EcoFlow says its Smart Home Panel 2 “requires installation before use,” and Anker says an electrician is required for the E10’s Power Dock or Smart Inlet Box. The upside: a lower starting price, and you can take the battery with you if you move.
 Do you need solar for a home battery?
 No. A home battery can charge from the grid and hold that energy until an outage. FranklinWH, for example, says the aPower 2 stores energy “from solar, grid, generator, and EV.” Every plug-in kit in our picks charges from a wall outlet too.
 What solar adds is staying power . Without it, a battery is a fixed tank: when it’s empty, it’s empty until the grid comes back. With solar, it refills on sunny days, so a long outage becomes a matter of using less at night rather than running out. Powerwall 3 has a solar inverter built in (up to 20 kW of panels on Tesla’s datasheet), and Enphase batteries are designed to work with Enphase microinverter solar. The plug-in kits take solar directly too: up to 5,600 W on the EcoFlow DELTA Pro Ultra and 9 kW on the Anker SOLIX E10, per their makers.
 Without solar you also give up most of the money-saving side, unless your utility has time-of-use rates or pays battery owners to share power at peak times. Our guide to the best home battery backup without solar goes through the options.
 Whole-home backup or essential loads?
 This is the biggest decision, and it drives both size and cost.
 Essential loads (partial backup): the installer moves your most important circuits (fridge, a few lights and outlets, Wi-Fi, furnace blower, sump or well pump) to a separate backup panel, or a smart panel picks them. The battery only feeds those. A smaller battery lasts days this way. The Jackery HomePower 3000 with a manual transfer switch (up to 6 circuits) and the EcoFlow Smart Home Panel 2 (12 circuits) work like this.
 Whole-home backup: the switching device sits between the meter and your main panel, so every circuit stays live. It’s simpler to live with, but the battery’s power limit still applies: an electric range, a dryer and central air all at once can overload it. Installers often add load controllers that shed big appliances during an outage. FranklinWH says one aPower 2 can power an entire home, including A/C, and Generac says PWRcell 2 supports whole-home backup up to 200 A service.
 Whole-home means every circuit is available, not that everything can run at once forever; runtime still depends on what you switch on.
 How to size a home battery: kWh and kW
 Sizing takes two numbers: energy (kWh) for how long, and power (kW) for what can run at the same time.
 List what must run. Fridge, freezer, lights, Wi-Fi, sump or well pump, furnace blower, medical devices. Decide whether you want anything big (central AC, an electric water heater, a well pump on 240 V).
 Add up energy per day. Use yearly kWh for fridges and freezers (from the ENERGY STAR label or the yellow EnergyGuide label), and watts × hours for everything else.
 Pick the outage length you want to ride out. One day? Three? Multiply. If you have solar, the battery only needs to cover the nights.
 Check power and starting surge. Add the watts of everything that could run at once and compare with the battery’s continuous kW. Motors (pumps, AC compressors) pull a big burst when they start; installers compare the motor’s locked-rotor amps (LRA) with the battery’s rating. Tesla lists 185 A LRA for Powerwall 3, FranklinWH 185 A for aPower 2, Anker 155 A for the E10 with two or more batteries, and Enphase up to 90 A for the IQ Battery 10C.
 Leave headroom. Batteries are often kept partly charged for daily savings, cold weather slows them, and plug-in units lose some energy in the inverter. We count 85% of a plug-in unit’s rated capacity as usable.

 Real homes vary a lot: a hot afternoon with central air running, or a cold night with electric heat, can empty a battery many times faster than the essentials line suggests. The practical answer for most families is to back up essentials for several days, or the whole home for a night, and add solar if outages last longer where you live. Our guide on how long a home battery lasts and how many batteries you need works through more examples.
 Two cheap tricks stretch any battery. Ready.gov says a closed fridge keeps food cold for about four hours and a full freezer holds its temperature for about 48 hours, so they don’t need power every minute. And turning off the biggest loads you don’t need (the water heater, the dryer, extra AC zones) buys hours.
 How much does a home battery backup cost in 2026?
 Installer systems: EnergySage says the average battery cost on its marketplace is $1,159 per kWh of stored energy, or $15,647 installed, based on quotes for a 13.5 kWh system like a Tesla Powerwall 3 (page updated August 2026). That’s before any state or local incentives. A second battery costs less per kWh than the first, because the gateway and much of the labor are already paid for, but installed prices vary widely by home and region. Get two or three quotes.
 Plug-in expandable kits (makers’ own prices, October 2026):

 Add the electrician’s work for the panel, dock or transfer switch, plus a permit where your town requires one. Ask for a written quote before you buy, because an older panel may need upgrades.
 Incentives: there’s no federal tax credit for a home battery installed in 2026; the 25D residential clean energy credit ended for installations completed after December 31, 2025. EnergySage notes you can still benefit from the business version of the credit indirectly if you lease a battery. Some states and utilities pay too. California’s SGIP closed its ratepayer-funded budgets at the end of 2025, while a state-funded budget for income-qualified homes continues. In Massachusetts, the Mass Save ConnectedSolutions program pays battery owners for sharing stored power during summer peaks. Many utilities run similar “virtual power plant” programs.  A standby generator wins on endurance: on a natural gas line it can run a whole house, central air included, for a week-long outage. Watch the ratings on gas, though: Generac’s 22 kW Guardian is rated 19.5 kW on natural gas. A home battery wins on quiet, zero maintenance, no fumes and everyday savings, and with solar it can ride out long outages too. Some homes combine both: Generac says PWRcell 2 can work with a Generac standby generator up to 28 kW. Read more in home battery backup vs generator and in our home generators guide .
 A portable power station is the low-cost entry point: no installation, safe indoors, and enough for a fridge and Wi-Fi for a day. See portable power stations and the best portable power station for home backup . The bigger ones blur into home batteries once you add a maker’s home panel.
 Installation and safety
 Anything connected to your house wiring is installed by a licensed electrician, with a permit where required. That covers installer systems and the panels, docks and transfer switches for plug-in kits.
 Never backfeed. Don’t plug a battery, power station or generator into a wall outlet with a double-ended cord. FEMA warns that power fed into a wall outlet can flow back onto utility lines and electrocute line workers or neighbors. CPSC adds that backfeeding bypasses some of your home’s built-in circuit protection.
 Look for safety listings. EcoFlow lists UL 9540 and UL 1973 for the DELTA Pro Ultra, and Enphase says the IQ Battery 10C was evaluated to UL 9540A. Your installer and local code decide where a battery may go (garage wall, outside wall, distance from doors and windows).
 Mind the temperature. Batteries have charging limits in the cold. Enphase lists –4°F to 122°F for charging the IQ Battery 10C. Plug-in units are usually kept indoors.
 Medical devices: if someone at home depends on oxygen, a CPAP or other equipment, talk to your doctor or equipment supplier about an outage plan, and tell your utility. Jackery, for example, says its power stations are not recommended for medical or life-support equipment.
 Batteries make no carbon monoxide, but generators do. If you also run a generator, CPSC says to run it outdoors only, at least 20 feet from the house, with the exhaust pointed away from the home, never in a garage, and to keep battery-powered CO alarms on every level.

 Home battery backup questions
 Can a home battery power my whole house?
 Yes, if it’s wired for whole-home backup and its power rating covers what runs at once. A 13.5 kWh battery runs an average home for roughly 11 hours by our estimate, and essentials for close to four days. Big loads like electric heat, ranges and central air drain it fast, so most whole-home systems use load management or more than one battery.
 How long does a home battery backup last?
 In an outage, divide usable kWh by your daily use: a 10 to 15 kWh battery covers about 3.5 kWh of daily essentials for roughly three to four days. Over its life, EnergySage says most batteries last about 10 to 15 years. Warranties differ: Tesla 10 years, Enphase and FranklinWH 15 years, each with its own capacity and energy limits.
 Do I need solar panels to get a home battery?
 No. Batteries charge from the grid and stand by for outages; FranklinWH, for example, stores energy from the grid, solar, a generator or an EV. Without solar, though, the battery can’t refill during a long outage, and you’ll save less money day to day unless your utility has time-of-use rates or a battery program.
 How much does a home battery backup cost?
 EnergySage’s 2026 average is about $1,159 per kWh installed, or $15,647 for a 13.5 kWh system, before incentives. Plug-in kits start lower: about $1,349 for a 3 kWh Jackery HomePower 3000 or about $4,199 for an EcoFlow DELTA Pro Ultra with one battery, plus an electrician for the home connection. Get two or three quotes.
 Is there a tax credit for home batteries in 2026?
 Not a federal one. The 30% residential clean energy credit (25D) ended for batteries and solar installed after December 31, 2025. Some states and utilities still offer rebates or pay battery owners to share power at peak times, such as Mass Save’s ConnectedSolutions in Massachusetts. Check DSIRE and your utility before you sign.
 Is a home battery better than a generator?
 It depends on your outages. A battery is silent, fume-free and switches on instantly, but it holds a fixed amount of energy unless you have solar. A natural gas standby generator runs a whole house for days, but needs fuel, maintenance and a safe outdoor spot. For frequent short outages, a battery suits most homes; for week-long ones without solar, a generator wins.
 Can I install a home battery myself?
 You can set up a plug-in battery and run appliances from it with cords. Connecting any battery to your home’s wiring (a panel, dock, inlet or transfer switch) must be done by a licensed electrician, with a permit where required. Installer systems like Powerwall, Enphase and FranklinWH are only sold and installed through the maker or certified installers.

 Want one battery that can run your whole house? FranklinWH is probably on your list.
 The FranklinWH aPower 2 is a 15 kWh home battery with 10 kW of continuous power, run by a controller called the aGate. Installed with new solar, it costs a median of about $17,250 on our marketplace, or about $1,150 for each kWh you can use. It fits homes that want whole-home backup, and homes adding a battery to solar they already have.

 What the numbers tell you:
 Adding it later costs a bit more. The same installer typically charges about $1,500 more to add an aPower 2 to existing solar, because the permits, inspection and labor aren't shared with a solar install.
 Extra batteries cost less than the first. The first battery's price covers the system around it, including the aGate. Two batteries with new solar come to about $930 per kWh.
 Is there still a federal tax credit for a FranklinWH battery?
 If you buy your battery (cash or loan), there's no federal tax credit in 2026. The homeowner credit ended at the end of 2025. When you add the battery with new solar, the way to still capture that value is a Prepaid TPO (a prepaid lease): a partner owns the system for the first five years, claims the business credit, and passes it to you as an upfront discount on your price. You own it after year five. How the Prepaid TPO works 
 A Prepaid TPO only covers equipment on the third-party owner's approved vendor list. As of October 2026, FranklinWH batteries aren't on our Prepaid TPO partners' lists, so on our marketplace a FranklinWH battery is a cash or loan purchase. If the Prepaid TPO discount matters to you, ask your installer about a battery that qualifies.
 Some utilities and states also offer battery rebates, such as California's SGIP program when funding is open. Your installer should check what applies at your address.
 Ready to see your numbers?
 See your real solar price in 90 seconds

 How the FranklinWH system works
 A FranklinWH system has two main parts: one or more aPower batteries, and the aGate controller, which serves as the system’s brain.
 The aGate: your whole-home backup switch
 The aGate connects your solar, the grid, your batteries and your home.
 In an outage, it disconnects your home from the grid and switches to battery power on its own. FranklinWH says always-on appliances, like the fridge and Wi-Fi router, aren't affected.
 Whole home or key circuits: it can back up the whole house from your service entrance, or feed a smaller backup panel. FranklinWH says its 280-amp capacity can help some homes skip a main panel upgrade.
 Add-ons: Smart Circuits let you schedule big loads, like an EV charger, or shut them off in an outage. A Generator module ties in a standby or portable generator.
 Warranty: 12 years, shorter than the battery's 15.
 Works with almost any existing solar
 The aPower 2 is AC-coupled: it has its own inverter and connects to your home's wiring next to your solar inverter. FranklinWH says the aGate works with both microinverters and string inverters, so the battery adds to most existing systems. Each conversion loses a little energy, and the aPower 2 gives back about 90% of what it stores.
 The aPower S takes power straight from your panels, so it fits best when you install solar and a battery together. Both can share one aGate. More in our inverter guide .
 What happens in an outage
 The switch is automatic. Owners who've been through outages say they barely notice it.
 It can run big loads. One aPower 2 supplies 10 kW continuously, and FranklinWH says it can start a 5-ton central air conditioner.
 How long it lasts depends on what you run. Roughly, 15 kWh runs 1 kW of essentials for about 15 hours, or central air drawing 4 kW for about 4.
 Solar refills it during the day. If it runs empty in a long outage, FranklinWH's black start feature lets solar charge it back up.
 The app
 The FranklinWH app shows your solar, battery and home use. You can set the battery to store solar for the evening, to run when your utility's rates are highest, or to stay full for outages. FranklinWH says it can also fully charge before severe weather.
 How FranklinWH compares

 What owners say about FranklinWH
 We read the reviews behind our California installer rankings : 158,781 published reviews of solar installers. More than 160 mention FranklinWH, across more than 60 installers, and most were written in 2025 and 2026. They average 4.8 stars, and more than 9 in 10 give five stars. Those stars rate the installer's whole job, not the battery.
 What came up most:
 Outages: owners who've been through them describe a switch they barely notice. The lights don't flicker and the Wi-Fi and freezer stay on. Some only learned about an outage from the app's alert.
 The app: when owners bring it up, it's almost always praise: easy to use, full of detail, with simple schedules. Good installers walk you through it before they leave.
 Install time: the work at your home usually takes one to three days. The wait is for permits, inspection and the utility's approval, which can take weeks or months.
 Service after the install: the best stories are about quick fixes. The few low-star reviews were about installers, not the battery: missed permit steps, setup errors, an unfinished utility hookup or an app login never handed over.
 Adding to existing solar: many reviewers added FranklinWH to solar they already had, including some whose original solar company went out of business.
 One thing to ask about: a couple of owners with Enphase microinverters had monitoring glitches after the battery went in, which their installers fixed. If you have Enphase micros, ask how your installer will handle it.
 The takeaway: as with any battery, who installs it matters as much as which battery you pick.
 FranklinWH pros and cons
 Pros: 
 15 kWh capacity and 10 kW continuous power in one battery: enough for whole-home backup in most homes, including some central air.
 Adds to almost any existing solar system.
 A 15-year warranty that covers up to 60 MWh, or about 4,000 full charges.
 Generator and smart-circuit options built into the aGate.
 Room to grow: up to 15 batteries on one aGate.
 Owners like the app.
 Cons: 
 A higher price up front than a Powerwall 3 on our marketplace, though the two are close per kWh.
 Fewer installers to choose from: about 4 in 10 installers on our marketplace that sell batteries list FranklinWH, against about 6 in 10 for the Powerwall 3 and more than 8 in 10 for Enphase.
 Big and heavy: 357 pounds and about 45 by 30 inches, so it needs a garage wall, an outside wall or floor space.
 The aGate's 12-year warranty is shorter than the battery's.
 FranklinWH is a younger company. We know of no financial problems, but long-term app and warranty support is worth weighing with any newer battery maker.
 Who the FranklinWH battery fits
 You want whole-home backup, including central air. One aPower 2 with an aGate covers most homes. Add a second for long outages or big loads.
 You already have solar. The aPower 2 works with almost any inverter. Expect to pay a bit more than adding it with new solar.
 You're installing solar and a battery together. Compare the aPower 2, the aPower S and the other batteries in our best batteries guide .
 You want backup for long outages. The aGate's Generator module ties in a generator.
 You mostly want a lower bill and rarely lose power. A smaller battery, or one without backup, may cost less. See backup vs no-backup batteries , or try our interactive battery explainer on your utility's rates.
 Your garage gets very hot or cold. The aPower 2 runs from −4°F to 122°F, and up to 131°F at reduced power.

 For an aPower 2, the median on our installers' price lists is about $19,000. That's typically about $1,500 more than the same installer charges with new solar, because the permits, inspection and labor aren't shared.
 Are FranklinWH batteries any good?
 On paper, the aPower 2 is one of the most capable home batteries: 15 kWh, 10 kW of continuous power, LFP cells and a 15-year warranty. Reviews that mention FranklinWH are very positive, but those stars rate installers, not the battery. Most problems we read about were installation or setup errors.
 Is FranklinWH better than Tesla?

The best home battery backup systems in 2026, and what they cost - Energy Collective 
 Skip to content 
 A home battery backup is a battery wired into your house that keeps the power on when the grid goes down, and the average installed system on EnergySage’s marketplace cost $15,650 before incentives in the first half of 2026. Our pick for most homes is the Tesla Powerwall 3, which typically installs for $13,473 , about 13% below the average battery there. For backup on the circuits you pick, EcoFlow’s Delta Pro 3 kit with a smart subpanel costs $4,189. Homeowners who buy a battery in 2026 get no federal tax credit , though a few state and utility programs still pay toward one.
 Tesla Powerwall 3 for most homes that want the whole house backed up
 FranklinWH aPower 2 for keeping central AC and a water heater running in an outage
 Enphase IQ Battery 5P and 10C for homes that already have Enphase microinverters
 Generac PWRcell 2 for homes already on Generac equipment
 EcoFlow Delta Pro Ultra for starting small and scaling up to whole-home backup
 EcoFlow Delta Pro 3 with Smart Home Panel 2 for backing up the circuits you pick without a full installed battery system
 EcoFlow prices on this page are the maker’s US store price in September 2026. These brands discount often, so the price moves. The four installed batteries are priced by installer quote.
 What a home battery backup costs in 2026
 The average home battery system on EnergySage’s marketplace cost $15,650 before incentives in the first half of 2026. Where you live changes how much a home battery costs, with a typical system averaging anywhere from $10,274 in Arkansas to $18,414 in Wyoming. Equipment makes up 50% to 60% of the total, so 40% to 50% of the bill goes to everything other than the hardware.
 Quotes are easiest to compare by cost per kWh. Across the top 10 brands EnergySage tracks, that figure runs from $342 to $3,505 per kWh. In EnergySage’s 2026 ranking , the Powerwall 3 averages $998 per kWh and the FranklinWH aPower 2 averages $1,177. The two EcoFlow picks are sold as hardware, at $4,189 for the Delta Pro 3 kit and $4,199 for the Delta Pro Ultra base unit , EcoFlow’s US store prices in September 2026.
 Homeowners who buy a battery in 2026 get no federal tax credit. The 30% Residential Clean Energy Credit, Section 25D, isn’t available for property placed in service after December 31, 2025 . Leasing works differently. A company that owns a battery and leases it to you, or sells you its output, can still claim the business credit under Section 48E, because the new 48E deadlines for solar and wind don’t apply to storage and the law didn’t ban leased systems. The credit belongs to the company, so ask any lease provider whether it shows up in your price.
 California’s Self-Generation Incentive Program pays per watt-hour of storage. As of September 2026, the general-market rate for home batteries steps down through funding tranches from $0.50 to $0.20 per Wh as money is claimed. The Equity budget pays $1.10 per Wh, and the Equity Resiliency budget pays $1.00 per Wh to customers in high fire-threat areas or those hit by Public Safety Power Shutoffs.
 Massachusetts and Hawaii pay by the kilowatt instead. National Grid’s ConnectedSolutions program in Massachusetts pays $275 per kW of your battery’s average performance from June 1 to September 30, which comes to about $1,200 a year for a typical battery. The rate is locked for your first five summers. In Hawaii, the Battery Bonus program closed to new participants on July 1, 2024 . Hawaiian Electric’s current program, Bring Your Own Device Plus, pays $400 per kW you commit, with no cap , and low- and moderate-income customers get another $400 per kW. BYOD Plus adds a monthly export credit, though NEM and NEM Plus customers don’t get it.
 How much battery your home needs
 The average US home used 10,791 kWh of electricity a year, or about 899 kWh a month . Divided by 365, that’s about 29.6 kWh a day , or roughly 1.23 kWh an hour. A single Powerwall 3 holds 13.5 kWh , a bit under half of an average day. Two FranklinWH aPower 2 units at 15 kWh each cover a full average day with a little to spare.
 Counting major events, the average US customer had 1.4 interruptions totaling 5.6 hours in 2022 , according to EIA. At 1.23 kWh an hour, 5.6 hours of average use comes to about 6.9 kWh, which one Powerwall 3 covers about twice over. EIA’s 2023 figure of about 2 hours across 1.3 interruptions leaves major events out, so it measures something different and can’t be set against the 2022 number.
 A critical-loads setup backs up only the circuits you choose, which shrinks the power you need. A refrigerator runs at about 700 W and a half-horsepower furnace blower at about 800 W , per SizeMyHome’s appliance chart, so the pair needs 1,500 W, well inside the Delta Pro 3’s 4,000 W. A 2-ton central AC is the load that pushes you toward whole-home backup. It runs at about 3,800 W and needs about 5,800 W to start, so it nearly fills a 4,000 W plug-in system by itself, while the Powerwall 3’s 11.5 kW continuous rating covers even its starting draw.
 Whole-home batteries versus plug-in battery backup
 The difference is how much of your house runs at once. A whole home battery backup carries the full house at the same time, up to its power rating, which is 11.5 kW continuous for the Powerwall 3 and 10 kW for the aPower 2. Generac rates the PWRcell 2 for whole-home backup up to 200 amps , and Enphase batteries need an IQ Meter Collar to back up a full home.
 A plug-in setup pairs a portable battery with a smart subpanel. EcoFlow’s Smart Home Panel 2 takes over 12 circuits and switches them to battery in 20 milliseconds , and the battery’s output caps how many of those circuits can run together. The panel still gets wired to your home’s main electrical panel, and EcoFlow’s store offers to connect you with a local electrician for that job. The Delta Pro Ultra gives you a path to whole-home backup without buying a full installed system on day one.
 Home battery backup without solar works with either type. Every pick on this list charges from the grid, so panels are optional. If you have solar or plan to add it, the Powerwall 3 is the one with a built-in solar inverter, which lets a new array feed it DC power directly, and it can also run AC-coupled beside an existing inverter. The other installed picks connect on the AC side. For the basics of how these batteries store and release power, see battery energy storage systems .
 If all you want is a fridge and a phone charger through a short outage, a portable power station on its own may cover it.

 Tesla Powerwall 3
 Our pick for most homes that want the whole house backed up. 
 The Tesla Powerwall 3 earns the top slot on price and power. EnergySage’s marketplace data puts its typical installed cost at $13,473, or $998 per kWh , about 13% below the average battery sold there, and it runs 11.5 kW continuously from 13.5 kWh of storage. It charges from the grid if you don’t have solar, and its built-in solar inverter can take DC power straight from a new array.
 The Powerwall 3 isn’t part of the CPSC recall announced November 13, 2025 , which covers about 10,500 older Powerwall 2 units sold from November 2020 to December 2022 over a fire hazard.
 The drawback is that Tesla publishes no US list price, so you won’t know your cost until you get quotes, and EnergySage’s state averages for a typical battery system range from $10,274 to $18,414.

 FranklinWH aPower 2
 Best if your central AC and water heater have to keep running when the grid is down. 
 FranklinWH built the aPower 2 to carry heavy loads like AC and water heaters through an outage, and EnergySage names it the battery with the highest peak power in its 2026 ranking. Each unit holds 15 kWh and runs 10 kW continuously, with bursts to 15 kW for 10 seconds and 25 kW for one second. You can link up to 15 units on one aGate for 225 kWh, the highest ceiling on this list, and the warranty runs 15 years or 60 MWh of throughput.
 FranklinWH doesn’t publish a price, and EnergySage’s data puts the aPower 2 at $1,177 per kWh, about 18% more than the Powerwall 3’s $998.

 Enphase IQ Battery 5P and 10C
 For homes that already make power with Enphase microinverters. 
 Both Enphase batteries here carry their own microinverters and connect on the AC side. The IQ Battery 5P holds 5 kWh and delivers 3.84 kW continuously, which lets you build up capacity in 5 kWh steps. The IQ Battery 10C holds 10 kWh at 7.08 kW in one box. Both carry a 15-year or 6,000-cycle warranty with at least 60% of capacity left at the end, tied with FranklinWH for the longest term here. Full-home backup takes an added IQ Meter Collar.
 Enphase publishes no limit on how many batteries you can stack and no prices, so the size and cost of a big system depend on how an installer designs it.
 Usable capacity: 5 kWh or 10 kWh
 Continuous power: 3.84 kW or 7.08 kW
 Warranty: 15 years or 6,000 cycles

 Generac PWRcell 2
 A fit for homes that already run a Generac standby generator or PWRmanager. 
 Rated for whole-home backup up to 200 amps, the Generac PWRcell 2 comes from the same lineup as Generac’s standby generators and PWRmanager. Each cabinet holds 9 kWh in the base M3 setup, and two cabinets reach 36 kWh. Continuous output runs from 5.2 kW on the M3 up to 11.5 kW. Generac rates a PWRcell 2 combined with AC-coupled solar at up to 26.5 kW of backup power.
 The PWRcell 2 tops out at 36 kWh, the lowest published limit among the installed batteries here and far under FranklinWH’s 225 kWh, which makes it a poor fit for multi-day backup in a large home.
 Usable capacity: 9 to 36 kWh

 Warranty: 10 years or 7.56 MWh
 Price: installer quote
 EcoFlow Delta Pro Ultra
 Suited to buyers who want to start with one unit and build toward whole-home backup later. 
 Of the whole-home-capable batteries here, only the EcoFlow Delta Pro Ultra has a price on the maker’s own store. The base unit costs $4,199 on EcoFlow’s US store in September 2026, and it holds 6.144 kWh. Adding battery packs takes it to 90 kWh with 15 of them. One inverter puts out 7.2 kW continuous and 10.8 kW peak, and more inverters stretch the range to 21.6 kW.
 It charges from the grid or a generator and pairs with EcoFlow’s Smart Home Panel 2. EcoFlow calls it the only portable power station certified to both UL1973 and UL9540.
 Its 5-year warranty is the shortest among the whole-home-capable picks, against 10 years for the Powerwall 3 and 15 for the aPower 2.
 Usable capacity: 6.144 kWh, up to 90 kWh
 Continuous power: 7.2 kW per inverter
 Warranty: 5 years
 Price: $4,199, EcoFlow’s US store price in September 2026
 EcoFlow Delta Pro 3 with Smart Home Panel 2
 The pick for backing up the circuits you care about most, with no whole-home install. 
 This EcoFlow Delta Pro 3 with Smart Home Panel 2 kit pairs a portable battery with a subpanel that takes over 12 circuits you pick and switches them to battery in 20 milliseconds when the grid drops. The battery holds 4.096 kWh to start and grows to 36 kWh with three units and six extra batteries. It charges from the wall without solar. The kit costs $4,189, plus an electrician to wire the panel to your main panel, which EcoFlow’s store can arrange.
 At 4,000 W continuous, it can’t run a central AC alongside much else, since a 2-ton unit alone runs at about 3,800 W .
 Usable capacity: 4.096 kWh, up to 36 kWh
 Continuous power: 4,000 W
 Price: $4,189 for the kit
 Battery backup versus a generator
 A generator costs less to install. Angi puts typical installed costs at $1,512 to $8,803, with a national average around $5,157 , and its whole-house tier of 22 to 48 kW at $5,000 to $18,000. EnergySage’s battery average is $15,650 . The two figures come from different sources, so the comparison is rough, but the average battery system costs about three times the average generator install.
 The generator keeps costing money after that. Angi estimates a 15 to 20 kW unit costs $90 to $220 a day to run, with annual fuel at $2,000 to $21,000 for natural gas or propane and $3,000 to $20,000 for diesel. A battery burns no fuel and refills from the grid or your solar once power is back.
 A generator wins on runtime, since it keeps going for as long as it has fuel. A 13.5 kWh Powerwall 3 lasts about 11 hours at the average home’s 1.23 kWh an hour, longer if you cut back to critical loads or stack more batteries.
 What would change the answer
 At 30% , the federal credit that ended with 2025 would be worth about $4,700 on the $15,650 average system . That’s money a 2026 buyer now pays out of pocket. If you lease, the company that owns the battery can still claim Section 48E, and it’s up to the lease terms whether any of that reaches you.
 State and utility programs can close part of the gap. In Massachusetts, the typical $1,200 a year from ConnectedSolutions adds up to about $6,000 over the five summers with a locked rate. In Hawaii, committing 5 kW from a 15 kWh battery to BYOD Plus earns $2,000 at $400 per kW , and Hawaiian Electric’s own example puts that setup’s export credit at about $52 a month.
 Base Power is a Texas-only option that installs and keeps ownership of a 39.2 kWh battery at your home for a $695 install fee plus $19 a month, and you buy your electricity from Base at its own rate. It makes its money sending that battery’s power to the grid during peak demand.

Best Home Batteries for Backup Power in 2026 · Solar Examiner Photo by Christian Buehner on Unsplash Key takeaways
 Backup power is a two-number problem: kW (how much you can run at once) and kWh (how long). A battery with big kWh and small kW can still trip when the air conditioner starts.
 Of the batteries compared here, the Powerwall 3 lists 11.5 kW continuous and the aPower 2 lists 10 kW; the Enphase IQ Battery 10C lists 7.08 kW and the IQ Battery 5P lists 3.84 kW.
 The federal residential clean energy credit does not apply to batteries placed in service after December 31, 2025, so budget at full price unless a state or utility program applies.
 Our picks come from manufacturer specs, certifications, warranties and published expert analysis. We did not test these batteries.
 Contains affiliate links. Solar Examiner may earn a commission if you buy through links marked “Check price.” Commissions do not affect which products we pick. See our affiliate disclosure and how we pick products .
 The best home battery for backup power is the one whose continuous output (kW) covers the loads you run at the same time and whose capacity (kWh) covers the hours you want to ride through. Among the batteries we reviewed, the Tesla Powerwall 3 and FranklinWH aPower 2 offer the highest output from a single unit, and Enphase IQ Batteries are the most modular. All figures below come from manufacturer documents or the published analyses we name, as of October 24, 2026.
 We have not tested these batteries. Our picks rest on specs, certifications, warranties and published expert and installer-marketplace analyses. See how we pick products .
 Quick picks
 Best for Pick Capacity Continuous power Warranty 
 Most output from one unit Tesla Powerwall 3 13.5 kWh (nominal) 11.5 kW 10 years 
 Largest single-unit capacity, rugged outdoor install FranklinWH aPower 2 15 kWh 10 kW 15 years / 60 MWh 
 Midsize modular backup Enphase IQ Battery 10C 10 kWh 7.08 kW 15 years / 6,000 cycles 
 Starting small, adding later Enphase IQ Battery 5P 5.0 kWh 3.84 kW 15 years / 6,000 cycles 
 Sources: Tesla Powerwall 3 datasheet (nominal energy; the datasheet does not state usable energy), FranklinWH aPower 2 product page (15 kWh stated without specifying usable), Enphase IQ Battery 10C and IQ Battery 5P .
 What does a backup battery actually have to do?
 Two numbers decide backup performance:
 Power (kW): the most the battery can deliver at one moment. Add up everything that might run together: refrigerator, lights, internet, well pump, furnace blower, an air conditioner.
 Energy (kWh): how long that power lasts. Hours of backup = usable kWh ÷ average kW load.
 Example (an illustration with assumed numbers, not a measurement): a home that averages 1.5 kW of essential loads for a 12-hour overnight outage needs 1.5 × 12 = 18 kWh. One 13.5 kWh battery would run out in about 9 hours (13.5 ÷ 1.5) before any solar recharge. See how to size a home battery for the full method, and our earlier battery sizing guide for a lighter-load example.
 Product cards
 Tesla Powerwall 3 — best for high output from one unit
 Tesla’s datasheet lists 13.5 kWh nominal energy, 11.5 kW maximum continuous discharge, a 10-year warranty, an operating range of -4°F to 122°F (derating possible above 104°F) and up to 20 kW of solar input across six MPPTs. It lists UL 1741, UL 9540, UL 9540A and UL 1973 among its certifications. Tesla’s own product page says it includes an integrated solar inverter.
 Pros 
 Highest continuous output of the batteries we compared.
 Integrated inverter means one box can handle solar and storage in a new install.
 Broad UL certification list on the datasheet.
 Cons 
 Shortest warranty of the four (10 years).
 Datasheet states nominal, not usable, energy.
 Tesla’s public pages do not list a price; installed cost varies by installer.
 Approximate price: EnergySage’s April 2026 battery ranking lists $998 per kWh; Solar.com’s battery guide reports a median of about $15,000 installed with solar (September 2026 installer price lists, before incentives). Prices checked October 24, 2026.
 Check price 
 FranklinWH aPower 2 — best for capacity and tough sites
 FranklinWH’s product page lists 15 kWh capacity, 10 kW continuous power, a 15-year warranty covering 60 MWh of throughput, IP67 dust and water protection, LFP chemistry and an operating range of -4°F to 131°F. It says up to 15 units can stack per aGate controller. The page does not state peak power or a UL 9540 listing, so ask your installer for the certification documents.
 Pros 
 Largest single-unit capacity here.
 Long warranty and an IP67 rating.
 FranklinWH says a single unit can start a 5-ton air conditioner.
 Cons 
 Certifications are not stated on the product page we read.
 The page does not say whether 15 kWh is usable energy.
 Uses FranklinWH’s own aGate controller, so it is a different ecosystem from Tesla or Enphase.
 Approximate price: EnergySage lists $1,177 per kWh; Solar.com reports about $17,250 median installed with solar (before incentives). Prices checked October 24, 2026.
 Check price 
 Enphase IQ Battery 10C — best for midsize modular backup
 Enphase’s product page lists 10 kWh, 7.08 kW continuous power and a 15-year warranty covering up to 6,000 cycles. It cites UL 9540A certification. A third-party comparison from NuWatt Energy describes it as AC-coupled and best suited to homes already using Enphase microinverters; we did not confirm the coupling on Enphase’s own page.
 Pros 
 Long warranty for the capacity.
 Modular: more units can be added.
 Natural fit with Enphase microinverter systems.
 Cons 
 Lower continuous power than a single Powerwall 3 or aPower 2.
 The Enphase page does not state operating temperature.
 Highest per-kWh price among the batteries EnergySage ranks here (see below).
 Approximate price: EnergySage lists $1,404 per kWh; Solar.com reports about $14,250 median installed with solar. Prices checked October 24, 2026.
 Check price 
 Enphase IQ Battery 5P — best for starting small
 The IQ Battery 5P lists 5.0 kWh usable capacity, 3.84 kW continuous power, 7.68 kW peak for 3 seconds and 6.14 kW for 10 seconds, six embedded grid-forming microinverters and a 15-year warranty up to 6,000 cycles. Backup requires an IQ System Controller 3 or 3G, and commissioning requires an Enphase-certified installer.
 Pros 
 Small steps: add units as budget allows.
 Enphase states usable (not nominal) capacity.
 Cons 
 You may need several units for whole-home backup, and the controller adds cost.
 Solar.com’s median for a no-backup version is about $6,125, but about $10,650 with backup, so the backup hardware matters.
 Check price 
 What about owner reviews?
 We looked for large, independent owner-satisfaction data on the batteries themselves and did not find a source we trust. Solar.com’s analysis covered 158,781 Google and Yelp reviews of California solar installers, 8,124 of which mention a battery, but it says those ratings reflect installer performance, not battery quality. Treat installer reputation as its own decision, and see how to compare solar quotes .
 Who should skip a battery
 Outages are rare and short. A battery is expensive insurance. If you mostly need to keep a phone, router and refrigerator going, a smaller system, or no battery, may do.
 You are on a flat rate with generous net metering. A battery adds little bill savings there. See net metering by state .
 You plan to run a large well pump or central air for days. Batteries ride through outages; they do not replace a generator for multi-day events unless sized and recharged by solar.
 You expect a federal tax credit. The credit for batteries placed in service after December 31, 2025 has ended (below).
 Incentives: what changed
 The IRS says the residential clean energy credit is not available for property placed in service after December 31, 2025. Storage of at least 3 kWh used to qualify. State incentives, utility battery programs and different rules for leased systems may still apply. Check your state’s page in Rates by State and ask your installer for the written basis of any incentive they quote. Confirm eligibility with a qualified tax professional.
 Buying checklist
 Critical loads and their kW. List what must run at once, including starting surges.
 Hours of backup. Hours = usable kWh ÷ average kW.
 Existing solar. Same-brand microinverters or a new hybrid system change which battery fits.
 Budget at full price. Get at least three written quotes with equipment model numbers.
 Climate and location. Compare operating temperature ranges and outdoor ratings.
 Warranty. Compare years and any cycle or throughput cap.
 Utility rules. Interconnection approval and export rules vary by utility; see our rate and policy guides .
 Certifications. Ask for UL 9540 documentation for the exact model.
 Limitations
 Figures are manufacturer-stated, sometimes nominal rather than usable, and prices are approximate installed medians or per-kWh figures from marketplaces, not quotes. Prices vary by home, utility and installer. This is not tax or engineering advice.

 Frequently asked questions
 What is the best home battery for backup power?
 For a single unit that can carry most of a home, the Tesla Powerwall 3 (11.5 kW continuous, 13.5 kWh nominal) and FranklinWH aPower 2 (10 kW continuous, 15 kWh) have the highest output of the batteries we reviewed. Enphase IQ Batteries are better when you want to add capacity in small steps or already have Enphase microinverters.
 How many batteries do I need to back up a whole house?
 It depends on the loads you want to run at once (kW) and for how long (kWh). Add up the loads, divide your target energy by one battery's capacity and round up. Our battery sizing guide walks through the formula.
 Is there still a federal tax credit for home batteries?
 The IRS says the residential clean energy credit is not available for property placed in service after December 31, 2025. State, local and utility programs may still apply. Confirm eligibility with a qualified tax professional.
 Can a home battery run central air conditioning?
 Sometimes. Starting a compressor needs a short surge well above its running power. Tesla's datasheet lists the ability to start loads up to 185 LRA, and FranklinWH says the aPower 2 can start a 5-ton A/C. Confirm your specific unit's starting current with your installer.
