Tesla Powerwall vs Enphase IQ Battery vs FranklinWH: Which Should You Buy? · Solar Examiner Photo by HUUM on Unsplash Key takeaways
 On published specs, the Powerwall 3 has the highest continuous output (11.5 kW), the aPower 2 the largest single-unit capacity (15 kWh) and a 15-year warranty, and Enphase IQ Batteries scale in 5 to 10 kWh steps.
 The Powerwall 3 has the shortest warranty of the group at 10 years; both FranklinWH and Enphase list 15 years with throughput or cycle limits.
 Per-kWh prices in EnergySage's April 2026 ranking run from $998 (Powerwall 3) to $1,404 (IQ Battery 10C), but your installed price depends on your home and installer.
 We compared specs and published analyses; we did not test any of these batteries.
 Contains affiliate links. Solar Examiner may earn a commission if you buy through links marked “Check price.” Commissions do not affect which products we pick. See our affiliate disclosure and how we pick products .
 Buy the Tesla Powerwall 3 if you want the most continuous power from one unit, the FranklinWH aPower 2 if you want the biggest single battery with a 15-year warranty, and an Enphase IQ Battery if you want to add capacity in small steps or already run Enphase microinverters. These are our reading of manufacturer documents and published analyses as of October 24, 2026. We did not test any of them. See how we pick products .
 Side-by-side
 Spec Powerwall 3 FranklinWH aPower 2 Enphase IQ Battery 10C Enphase IQ Battery 5P 
 Capacity 13.5 kWh (nominal) 15 kWh 10 kWh 5.0 kWh (usable) 
 Continuous power 11.5 kW 10 kW 7.08 kW 3.84 kW 
 Peak power Starts loads to 185 LRA (no kW peak stated) Not stated; says it can start a 5-ton A/C Not stated 7.68 kW (3 s), 6.14 kW (10 s) 
 Warranty 10 years 15 years, 60 MWh 15 years, 6,000 cycles 15 years, 6,000 cycles 
 Operating temp. -4°F to 122°F -4°F to 131°F Not stated on page Not stated on page 
 Solar input Integrated inverter, up to 20 kW STC See installer AC-coupled (per third party) AC-coupled 
 Stacking Multiple units Up to 15 per aGate (225 kWh) Modular Modular 
 Approx. $/kWh (EnergySage, Apr 2026) $998 $1,177 $1,404 not listed 
 Sources: Tesla datasheet , FranklinWH , Enphase 10C , Enphase 5P , EnergySage (updated Apr 29, 2026). A third-party comparison by NuWatt Energy describes the 10C as AC-coupled; we did not confirm that on Enphase’s page. “Not stated” means the manufacturer page we read did not state it, not that the product lacks it.
 Which should you buy?
 If you want the most power from one box: Powerwall 3
 Its 11.5 kW continuous discharge is the highest here, and the datasheet lists UL 1741, UL 9540, UL 9540A and UL 1973. Tesla’s page says the unit includes an integrated solar inverter, and the datasheet lists up to 20 kW of PV input. In a new solar-plus-storage install that can mean fewer boxes. The trade-off is the 10-year warranty, five years shorter than the other two.
 Check Powerwall 3 price 
 If you want capacity and a long warranty: aPower 2
 FranklinWH lists 15 kWh, 10 kW continuous, 15 years or 60 MWh, and IP67 protection. Its stacking limit of 15 units per aGate gives a ceiling of 225 kWh. The product page we read did not state a UL listing; ask for the document for the exact model.
 Check aPower 2 price 
 If you want modular steps or already have Enphase: IQ Battery
 The 5P adds 5.0 kWh and 3.84 kW per unit; the 10C adds 10 kWh and 7.08 kW. Both carry a 15-year warranty up to 6,000 cycles. The 5P requires an IQ System Controller 3 or 3G for backup and Enphase-certified commissioning. Per kWh, EnergySage lists the 10C at the highest price of the batteries in its table, so compare full quotes, not spec sheets.
 Check IQ Battery price 
 Price check
 EnergySage’s per-kWh figures (Apr 2026) are $998 for Powerwall 3, $1,177 for aPower 2 and $1,404 for IQ Battery 10C. Solar.com’s September 2026 installer price lists show medians of about $15,000 (Powerwall 3), $17,250 (aPower 2) and $14,250 (IQ Battery 10C) installed with solar, before incentives. These are marketplace medians and per-kWh averages, not quotes, and the 10C is smaller, so a lower total can still mean a higher price per kWh. Prices checked October 24, 2026.
 Worked example (our math): $998 per kWh × 13.5 kWh = $13,473 for a Powerwall 3 at EnergySage’s per-kWh figure; $1,404 × 10 kWh = $14,040 for one 10C. The 10C costs more in total for 3.5 kWh less capacity at those figures.
 Who should skip all three
 Homes with rare short outages and no time-of-use rate; a battery rarely pays back on bill savings alone.
 Buyers who need weeks of backup; solar recharge or a generator matters more than battery brand.
 Anyone counting on a federal credit; see below.
 Incentives
 The IRS says the residential clean energy credit is not available for property placed in service after December 31, 2025. State, local and utility programs vary; check Rates by State and your utility. Leased or financed arrangements can be taxed differently; ask the provider for the written basis.
 How to decide
 Decide required kW (loads at once) and kWh (hours). See how to size a home battery .
 If you already have Enphase microinverters, price an IQ Battery first; otherwise price all three.
 Ask each installer for model numbers, warranty documents and UL certification for the exact unit.
 Compare total installed price, not price per kWh alone.
 Read the time-of-use guide if your utility has peak pricing.
 Limitations
 Specs are manufacturer-stated and sometimes nominal rather than usable. We found no independent owner-satisfaction data for these batteries; the Solar.com review analysis rates installers, not products. This is not tax or engineering advice.
 Sources

 Frequently asked questions
 Which is better: Powerwall 3, Enphase IQ Battery or FranklinWH aPower 2?
 It depends on what you need. The Powerwall 3 has the highest continuous output (11.5 kW). The aPower 2 has the largest single-unit capacity (15 kWh) and a 15-year warranty. Enphase IQ Batteries add capacity in smaller steps and suit homes with Enphase microinverters.
 Do I need Enphase solar to use an Enphase battery?
 Not necessarily. Enphase has announced IQ Battery 10C support for existing third-party solar systems, but check compatibility and installer certification requirements for your exact setup.
 Which battery has the longest warranty?
 FranklinWH aPower 2 (15 years, 60 MWh throughput) and Enphase IQ Batteries (15 years, up to 6,000 cycles) both list 15 years. The Powerwall 3 lists 10 years.
 Are these batteries eligible for the federal tax credit?
 The IRS says the residential clean energy credit does not apply to property placed in service after December 31, 2025. State and utility programs may still apply; confirm with a tax professional.

 What extra hardware is needed, and is it in the quote? Gateways, controllers and smart panels are separate line items in many systems.
 Who installs it, who pulls the permit, and who services it in my area? Service coverage differs by address, and one company rarely covers every state.
 What does the warranty cover? Years, cycles or throughput, end capacity and labor all count.

Powerwall 3 vs Enphase 10C vs FranklinWH (2026) | OC Solar 
 Skip to content 
 Published July 16, 2026 · Updated September 22, 2026 · 9 min read
 The short answer
 Powerwall 3 (13.5 kWh, 11.5 kW, integrated solar inverter) wins most new-solar installs. FranklinWH aPower 2 (15 kWh, 10 kW) wins big AC-coupled retrofits. Enphase IQ 10C (10 kWh, 7.08 kW) wins microinverter homes. All three back up whole homes; architecture decides.
 By Vinnie Curcie , Founder & CEO, OC Solar
 The three home batteries that matter in 2026
 If you are shopping for a home battery in 2026, three products dominate the U.S. residential market: the Tesla Powerwall 3 , the Enphase IQ Battery 10C, and the FranklinWH aPower 2. All three use lithium iron phosphate (LFP) chemistry, all three are rated for outdoor installation, and all three can back up an entire home when sized and configured correctly. Beyond that, they diverge sharply — in how they connect to solar, how much power they deliver, how they scale, and how their warranties are written.
 A disclosure before the numbers: OC Solar is a Tesla Powerwall Premier Certified installer, and Powerwall is what most of our customers choose. We also believe a comparison is only useful if it is fair — Enphase and FranklinWH build excellent equipment, and there are homes where each is the better answer. Every specification below comes from the manufacturers' own 2025–2026 datasheets, linked in the sources, so you can check our work.
 This guide is the deep three-way comparison. If you only want Tesla-vs-Enphase, we keep a dedicated Enphase IQ Battery 10C vs Powerwall 3 head-to-head , and for full Powerwall pricing scenarios see our Tesla Powerwall cost guide for 2026 .
 Spec comparison: capacity, power, efficiency, warranty
 Here is how the three batteries compare on the numbers that actually drive sizing decisions, taken directly from each manufacturer's current datasheet.
 Tesla Powerwall 3 vs Enphase IQ Battery 10C vs FranklinWH aPower 2 — manufacturer datasheet specs (verified July 2026) Spec Tesla Powerwall 3 Enphase IQ Battery 10C FranklinWH aPower 2 
 Usable capacity 13.5 kWh 10.0 kWh 15 kWh 
 Continuous power 11.5 kW (on-grid and backup) 7.08 kW 10 kW / 11.5 kVA 
 Short-burst peak Not published (starts 185 LRA loads) 56 A for 3 s (~13.4 kVA) 15 kW for 10 s; 25 kW for 1 s 
 Motor start (LRA) 185 LRA Up to 90 A LRA 185 A LRA (off-grid) 
 Solar coupling DC-coupled, integrated hybrid inverter, 6 MPPTs, up to 20 kW solar AC-coupled, 4 embedded IQ8B microinverters AC-coupled (works with any inverter) 
 Efficiency 97.5% solar-to-home; 89% round trip 90% AC round trip (96% DC) 90% round trip 
 Chemistry LFP LFP LFP 
 Scalability Up to 4 units (54 kWh) Modular 10 kWh blocks Up to 15 units per aGate (225 kWh) 
 Warranty 10 years 15 years or 6,000 cycles (to 60% capacity) 15 years or 60 MWh throughput 
 Weight 287 lb 317 lb installed 357 lb 
 Sources: Tesla Powerwall 3 Datasheet (2024), Enphase IQ Battery 10C Data Sheet rev 9.0 (Feb 2026), FranklinWH aPower 2 Datasheet (Dec 2025). Peak and LRA figures are manufacturer ratings under their stated test conditions.
 The biggest difference: where the solar inverter lives
 The single most important architectural difference is invisible on a spec table. The Powerwall 3 has a full solar inverter built in — six MPPT circuits accepting up to 20 kW of solar DC directly. On a new installation, that means one box on the wall replaces a separate string inverter entirely, and solar power flows to your home at 97.5% efficiency without being converted to AC and back. That is why Powerwall 3 usually wins on total system cost for new solar-plus-battery projects: you are not buying an inverter twice.
 The Enphase IQ Battery 10C takes the opposite philosophy. It contains four embedded IQ8B microinverters and is AC-coupled, designed to pair with Enphase microinverters on the roof. There is no single point of failure — if one microinverter dies, the rest keep producing — and each battery is field-serviceable. For the roughly one-in-five homes we see with existing Enphase microinverter systems, staying in the Enphase ecosystem keeps monitoring, rapid shutdown, and warranty service under one app and one manufacturer.
 The FranklinWH aPower 2 is also AC-coupled but deliberately inverter-agnostic: it sits behind any existing solar inverter — string, micro, or hybrid — and its aGate controller manages the home. That makes it the retrofit specialist. If you installed solar five years ago with a SolarEdge or SMA inverter that still works fine, an aPower 2 adds storage without touching the existing array.
 Whole-home backup: can one battery really run your house?
 All three systems support whole-home backup, but the hardware path differs. Powerwall 3 pairs with the Tesla Backup Switch (installed behind the utility meter) or Gateway 3 for whole-home transfer; its 11.5 kW continuous output and 185 LRA motor-start rating mean a single unit can start and run most central air conditioners — the load that actually breaks most backup plans. Tesla publishes no burst kW rating, but in practice the LRA number is the one that matters for compressor starts.
 FranklinWH is the power heavyweight among AC-coupled options: 10 kW continuous with a 15 kW ten-second surge, a 25 kW one-second transient rating, and 185 A LRA start capability off-grid. Its aGate acts as the whole-home transfer switch and supports smart-circuit load management, so you can shed a pool pump or EV charger automatically when an outage runs long.
 The Enphase IQ 10C delivers 7.08 kW continuous with a 56 A three-second surge and up to 90 A LRA soft-start capability. Whole-home backup uses the IQ Meter Collar behind the meter plus the IQ Combiner 6C. One 10C comfortably backs up a typical home if you manage the AC with a soft starter or Enphase's power control; homes with large 5-ton compressors usually want two units. Enphase's counterargument is granularity: 10 kWh blocks let you size capacity more precisely than 13.5 or 15 kWh steps.
 Ready to apply this to your home, system, or project? Use the guided next step online; our local team is available whenever you want help.
 Size my home battery → What they cost in 2026 (and what happened to the tax credit)
 OC Solar's Tesla Powerwall 3 installation range is $9,995–$15,995, as of September 2026. $9,995 is for a basic installation with Participate Energy. Final pricing depends on the custom configuration and selected plan. Garage or outdoor placement, distance from the battery to the main service panel, whole-home or partial backup, and a Backup Switch or Gateway all affect the installation scope.
 Standalone battery permits can cost $1,000 or more, depending on the city's permitting fees. When batteries are installed with solar panels, battery permitting is often included in the solar permit cost. OC Solar confirms the local requirements and itemizes the permit allowance in your proposal.
 Our published comparison ranges for the other platforms remain $13,000–$17,000 for Enphase IQ Battery 10C with its Meter Collar and Combiner, and $15,000–$19,000 for FranklinWH aPower 2 with its aGate. The Powerwall starting price has a Participate Energy condition, so these are not identical cash-purchase offers. Compare plan terms, equipment and electrical scope in an itemized proposal. See the Powerwall cost guide for the detailed installation variables.
 VPP participation: getting paid for your battery
 In 2026, a battery that just sits waiting for an outage is leaving money on the table. California's Demand Side Grid Support (DSGS) program pays participants for upfront capacity commitments and per-unit reductions in net load during grid stress events, and all three manufacturers operate virtual power plant (VPP) enrollment paths into DSGS-style programs through their apps or aggregator partners. Tesla enrolls Powerwall owners through the Tesla app's VPP programs with the major California utilities; Enphase and FranklinWH batteries enroll through aggregators tied to their monitoring platforms. Note that SGIP rebate recipients are required to enroll in a qualifying demand response program within a year of reserving funds — VPP participation is becoming the default, not the exception.
 Practical differences: Tesla's VPP has the largest enrolled fleet and the most polished single-app experience. Enphase gives fine-grained reserve control (you set exactly how much capacity events may use). FranklinWH's aGate exposes smart-circuit controls that let an aggregator shed loads, not just discharge the battery. Earnings vary by utility, season, and event count, so treat any fixed dollar promise from a salesperson skeptically — program terms, not hardware, set the ceiling.
 What our 2025 install data says about which one to pick
 Our own install data is the strongest signal we can offer. Across the 1,299 projects and service calls OC Solar completed in 2025, 70% of our solar customers added battery storage — and 98% of the batteries we installed were Tesla Powerwalls, on a median system size of 8.0 kW of solar. That skew is partly because we quote Powerwall 3 aggressively as a Premier Certified installer, but mostly because the integrated inverter makes it the lowest-total-cost path for the new solar-plus-storage projects that dominate our pipeline under NEM 3.0.
 The pattern in the exceptions is just as instructive. The Enphase and FranklinWH systems we install are almost all retrofits: Enphase when the roof already runs IQ microinverters, FranklinWH when a customer wants maximum AC-coupled capacity (a single 15 kWh unit, scaling to 225 kWh) or aggressive load management behind a legacy inverter. Warranty preference occasionally decides it — buyers planning to cycle hard daily sometimes choose Enphase's or FranklinWH's 15-year terms over Tesla's 10 years.
 OC Solar is a Tesla Powerwall Premier Certified solar and battery installer headquartered at 240 Progress, Suite 100, Irvine, California, serving Orange County, Los Angeles, San Diego, Riverside, San Bernardino, and Ventura counties with 30+ megawatts installed. If you want a same-week answer on which of these three fits your panel, roof, and rate plan, our battery storage team will model all three against your actual usage — and show you the math either way.
 FAQ
 Which is better in 2026: Powerwall 3, Enphase IQ Battery 10C, or FranklinWH aPower 2? + For new solar-plus-battery installations, Powerwall 3 usually wins on total cost because its solar inverter is built in (13.5 kWh, 11.5 kW, 20 kW of solar input). For retrofits onto an existing Enphase microinverter system, the IQ Battery 10C is the cleanest fit. For adding maximum storage behind any existing inverter, the 15 kWh FranklinWH aPower 2 is the strongest AC-coupled option. All three use safe LFP chemistry and support whole-home backup.
 Can a Tesla Powerwall 3 run my whole house including air conditioning? + Usually yes. A single Powerwall 3 delivers 11.5 kW of continuous power and can start motor loads rated up to 185 LRA, which covers most residential central air conditioners. Runtime is the real constraint: 13.5 kWh of usable energy runs a typical home for an evening, so households wanting multi-day outage coverage or heavy AC use during outages often add a second unit or an expansion.
 How much do these home batteries cost installed in 2026? + OC Solar's Tesla Powerwall 3 installation range is $9,995–$15,995, as of September 2026. $9,995 is for a basic installation with Participate Energy. Final pricing depends on the custom configuration and selected plan. Garage or outdoor placement, distance from the battery to the main service panel, whole-home or partial backup, and a Backup Switch or Gateway all affect the installation scope. Compare the selected plan and included hardware with Enphase or FranklinWH proposals.
 Is there still a federal tax credit for home batteries in 2026? + Not for homeowner-purchased systems. The 30% Residential Clean Energy Credit (Section 25D) does not apply to property placed in service after December 31, 2025. Leased or PPA systems differ: the third-party owner may qualify for the separate Section 48E investment credit and pass savings through in pricing. California's SGIP rebate is still available in 2026, with the largest amounts reserved for equity and resiliency customers.
 Which battery has the best warranty: Tesla, Enphase, or FranklinWH? + On paper, Enphase and FranklinWH both offer 15-year warranties versus Tesla's 10 years. Enphase warrants the IQ Battery 10C for 15 years or 6,000 cycles to 60% remaining capacity. FranklinWH warrants the aPower 2 for 15 years or 60 MWh of throughput. Tesla's Powerwall 3 warranty is 10 years. Heavy daily cyclers get the most value from the 15-year terms; for typical backup-plus-TOU use, all three usually outlast their payback period.
 Do Enphase and FranklinWH batteries work with Tesla solar panels or any existing solar system? + Both are AC-coupled, so they can attach to almost any existing grid-tied solar system regardless of panel or inverter brand. FranklinWH is expressly inverter-agnostic and manages the home through its aGate controller. Enphase IQ Battery 10C works best paired with Enphase microinverters for unified monitoring and warranty. Powerwall 3 also AC-couples to existing solar, but its biggest advantage, the built-in solar inverter, only applies on new installations.
 Can I get paid for letting my battery join a virtual power plant in California? + Yes. California's Demand Side Grid Support program pays for capacity commitments and load reductions during grid stress events, and Tesla, Enphase, and FranklinWH all offer VPP enrollment through their apps or aggregator partners. If you take an SGIP rebate, enrolling in a qualifying demand response program is required within a year. Earnings depend on your utility and event frequency, so verify current program terms rather than relying on fixed dollar promises.

Home Battery Backup in California (2026): Cost and Sizing 
 Home Battery Backup in California (2026): Cost, Sizing, and Whether You Need Solar
 October 28, 2026 
 Quick answer: A home battery backup in California costs about $13,000 to $19,000 installed for one battery on a critical-loads panel, and about $23,000 to $44,000 for whole-home backup with 2 to 3 batteries, as of November 2026. One 13.5 kWh battery runs a fridge, lights, Wi-Fi and a gas furnace fan for about 24 to 36 hours. The federal 30% credit ended for homeowner systems installed after December 31, 2025, so plan on the full price unless you qualify for SGIP equity funding.
 Most people searching for home battery backup in California are not shopping for a gadget. They just got a PSPS notice, or their power went out for 14 hours in a wind event, or their utility bill doubled between 4 and 9 p.m. That is the first thing I tell homeowners here: in this state a battery has two jobs, keeping the lights on and dodging peak rates, and you should size it for the job you care about most.
 This guide covers what a home battery backup system costs in California right now, how many batteries you actually need, whether you can install one without solar, how the main models compare, and when a generator or a portable power station is the smarter buy.
 Key takeaways 
 One installed battery with a critical-loads panel: about $13,000 to $19,000. Whole-home backup with central AC: about $23,000 to $44,000.
 Size by daily kWh, not by house size. Most California critical-loads setups use 7 to 12 kWh a day, which one 13.5 to 15 kWh battery covers.
 You can install a battery without solar, but it only recharges from the grid, so a multi-day PSPS outage drains it for good.
 SGIP money remains only in the income-qualified equity budget, and most of it is waitlisted. The 25D federal credit ended for homeowner systems installed after December 31, 2025.
 Peak-rate savings are biggest on SDG&E, then SCE, and smallest on PG&E.
 What is a home battery backup system?
 A home battery backup system is a wall- or floor-mounted lithium battery, wired into your electrical panel, that switches on automatically within a fraction of a second when the grid goes down. It charges from solar panels, the grid, or both, and on normal days it can also discharge during your utility’s 4 to 9 p.m. peak window to cut your bill.
 Every permanent system has three parts: the battery itself, an inverter (built into most new batteries), and a gateway or automatic transfer switch that isolates your home from the grid during an outage. That isolation is a safety requirement, and it is why a real home battery backup needs a licensed electrician, a permit and a utility notification, unlike a plug-in power station.
 For the full picture on what goes into the price, see our breakdown of what a solar battery costs in California .
 How much does a home battery backup cost in California in 2026?
 One battery installed on a critical-loads panel costs about $13,000 to $19,000 in California as of November 2026. Whole-home backup that can run central air usually takes 2 or 3 batteries and lands around $23,000 to $44,000, depending on your main panel and the size of your AC.
 Home battery backup cost in California by backup level, November 2026 
 Backup level What it runs Typical runtime Installed cost 
 1 battery, critical loads Fridge, lights, Wi-Fi, phones, TV, gas furnace fan, garage door About 24 to 36 hours at 8 to 12 kWh a day $13,000 to $19,000 
 2 batteries, most of the home The above plus microwave, washer, well pump, a mini-split or window AC About 24 hours at 20 to 25 kWh a day $23,000 to $31,000 
 3 batteries, whole home Everything, including central AC for part of the afternoon About 24 hours at 30 to 40 kWh a day $33,000 to $44,000 
 Source: installed ranges from our current California quotes; runtimes calculated from usable capacity on the Tesla Powerwall 3 datasheet and the FranklinWH aPower 2 datasheet .
 Three things move a quote by thousands of dollars:
 A main panel upgrade. Older 100 A or 125 A panels often need an upgrade to 200 A for whole-home backup. That adds about $2,500 to $5,000.
 Permits and inspection. About $400 to $1,200 depending on the city and whether the fire department reviews the battery location.
 Distance from the panel. Long conduit runs or trenching add about $500 to $1,500.
 A second battery on the same job costs less than the first, about $10,000 to $12,500, because the gateway, permit and most of the labor are already paid for.
 Does the federal tax credit or SGIP still lower the price?
 For most California homeowners buying a battery in 2026, no. The federal Residential Clean Energy Credit (Section 25D) ended for systems installed (placed in service) after December 31, 2025, according to the IRS , so it does not apply to a battery installed this year.
 California’s Self-Generation Incentive Program (SGIP) still exists, but its general residential budget is closed. The money that remains is for income-qualified households only (at or below 80% of area median income, or enrolled in CARE, FERA or ESA), and much of it is waitlisted.
 SGIP residential storage status by utility (checked October 28, 2026) 
 SGIP budget PG&E SCE SoCalGas Rate 
 Small Residential Storage (general market) Closed Closed Closed $0.15 per Wh 
 Residential Solar and Storage Equity, AB 209 non-POU Waitlisted Waitlisted Not offered $1.10 per Wh 
 Residential Solar and Storage Equity, AB 209 POU Waitlisted Open Not offered $1.10 per Wh 
 San Joaquin Valley Residential Closed Closed Not offered $1.10 per Wh 
 Source: SGIP Program Metrics and the CPUC SGIP page . Budgets change often: check the dashboard on the day you apply.
 If you qualify for the equity budget, the math is dramatic: at $1.10 per Wh, a 13.5 kWh battery could earn up to about $14,850. That is worth applying for even with a waitlist. Just do not count it in your budget until you have a reservation confirmation in writing. Our plain-English guide to the Self-Generation Incentive Program walks through eligibility.
 How many batteries do I need to back up my house?
 Most California homes need one battery for critical loads and two to three batteries for whole-home backup with central air. Size by the kWh you need per day of outage, not by square footage: a 2,500 sq ft home with gas heat and no AC can use less than a 1,400 sq ft home with an EV and a pool pump.
 Start with your daily usage. If you do not know it, our guide to how many kWh per day is normal shows typical California numbers by home size. Then cut it down to what you would actually run during an outage.
 Daily outage load for a typical California critical-loads panel 
 Load Typical use per day 
 Refrigerator About 1.5 kWh 
 LED lights, TV, electronics About 2 to 3 kWh 
 Gas furnace blower (winter) About 2 kWh 
 Wi-Fi, phones, laptops About 0.5 kWh 
 Well pump or sump pump (if you have one) About 1 to 2 kWh 
 Total About 6 to 9 kWh 
 Source: appliance draws from manufacturer ratings and the U.S. Department of Energy appliance energy calculator ; totals are our sizing defaults.
 Two numbers decide the size:
 Capacity (kWh) sets how long you last. Divide your outage load by the battery’s usable kWh.
 Power (kW) sets what you can run at the same moment. A 3-ton central AC can pull 3 to 4 kW while running and much more for a second at startup. That startup surge is why we check your AC’s nameplate before promising whole-home backup.
 The takeaway: one 13.5 to 15 kWh battery is enough for most California critical-loads setups, and you only need a second or third battery when central AC or an EV is part of the plan. For appliance-by-appliance runtimes, see how long a solar battery can power a house .
 Can I get a home battery backup without solar?
 Yes. Most batteries we install, including the Tesla Powerwall 3 and FranklinWH aPower 2, can be installed without solar panels and charged from the grid. The tradeoff is that a battery-only system cannot recharge during an outage, so once it is empty, it stays empty until the grid comes back.
 That makes battery-only a good fit when:
 Your outages are short, a few hours to one day, and you mostly want the lights and the fridge to ride through.
 Your roof cannot take solar (shade, orientation, an HOA, or a roof that needs replacing soon).
 You are on a time-of-use plan with a wide gap between peak and off-peak rates, so charging at night and discharging from 4 to 9 p.m. pays you back.
 It is a weaker fit if you live in a PG&E or SCE fire-risk area where PSPS shutoffs can last two or three days. In that case, solar is what keeps the battery going: even a 6 kW array in winter can put about 15 to 20 kWh back into the battery on a clear winter day.
 If you are adding a battery to an existing solar system, ask about a meter collar adapter : on some homes it replaces a costly panel upgrade.
 Tesla Powerwall 3 vs Enphase IQ Battery 5P vs FranklinWH aPower 2
 The three batteries we install most in California are the Tesla Powerwall 3, the Enphase IQ Battery 5P and the FranklinWH aPower 2. Per usable kWh, the FranklinWH is usually the cheapest storage, the Powerwall 3 is the best value when you also need a solar inverter, and the Enphase 5P is the most modular.
 Home battery backup comparison, California installs, November 2026 
 Battery Usable capacity Continuous power Installed cost (1 unit) Warranty Best for 
 Tesla Powerwall 3 13.5 kWh 11.5 kW $13,000 to $16,500 10 years New solar plus battery, whole-home backup 
 FranklinWH aPower 2 15 kWh 10 kW $11,000 to $15,000 15 years or 60 MWh Adding storage to existing solar, lowest cost per kWh 
 Enphase IQ Battery 5P 5 kWh 3.84 kW $7,500 to $8,500 15 years Enphase microinverter homes, small critical-loads setups 
 Source: capacity, power and warranty from the Tesla Powerwall 3 datasheet , FranklinWH aPower 2 datasheet and Enphase IQ Battery 5P data sheet ; installed ranges from our California quotes.
 A few details matter more than the headline specs:
 Motor starting. Both the Powerwall 3 and the aPower 2 are rated to start loads up to 185 LRA, which covers most residential AC compressors and well pumps. We still check your nameplate.
 Expansion. Powerwall 3 supports up to 4 units. FranklinWH supports up to 15 aPower units per aGate, up to 225 kWh. Enphase stacks in 5 kWh steps. See our guide to the Powerwall 3 expansion pack if you plan to grow.
 Heat. Tesla rates the Powerwall 3 from -4°F to 122°F, with output possibly reduced above 104°F. In the Inland Empire and the Central Valley we often site batteries on a shaded wall or in the garage for that reason.
 Chemistry. The FranklinWH aPower 2 uses lithium iron phosphate (LFP), the chemistry favored for thermal stability.
 For head-to-head detail, read Tesla Powerwall vs Enphase and FranklinWH vs Tesla Powerwall , or our ranking of the best solar battery for your home .
 Does a home battery pay for itself in California?
 With solar on a time-of-use plan, a battery can pay back in about 8 to 12 years in California, fastest on SDG&E, then SCE, slowest on PG&E. Without solar, a battery is mostly a resilience purchase: the bill savings are real but rarely cover the cost within the warranty.
 The savings come from shifting stored solar into the 4 to 9 p.m. peak instead of exporting it. Under California’s net billing tariff, exported solar earns far less than the retail peak rate, which is why batteries matter so much more than they did under NEM 2.0.
 Simple battery payback by utility, one battery with solar 
 Utility and plan Average 4 to 9 p.m. rate Annual value of 3,300 kWh shifted Simple payback on $14,500 
 SDG&E TOU-DR1 64.7 cents $1,886 7.7 years 
 SCE TOU-D-PRIME 50.3 cents $1,413 10.3 years 
 PG&E E-TOU-C 43.9 cents $1,201 12.1 years 
 Source: peak rates from current tariff sheets as used in our solar battery cost guide ; export value under the CPUC net billing tariff . Annual value assumes the battery shifts about 10 kWh of solar a day on 330 days a year (3,300 kWh), minus about 7.5 cents per kWh of lost export value.
 Worked example. A 2,000 sq ft home in Sonoma County on PG&E gets a PSPS notice for a 24-hour shutoff. It has a 7 kW solar array and one Powerwall 3 on a critical-loads panel. The fridge (1.5 kWh), lights and electronics (3 kWh), gas furnace blower (2 kWh) and Wi-Fi and phones (0.5 kWh) total about 7 kWh for the day. The battery covers that with about half its charge left, and on a clear October day the panels refill it by mid-afternoon. On normal days, the same battery shifts about 10 kWh into PG&E’s peak window. At $14,500 installed with no incentive, that is a payback of about 12 years, plus a home that stays lit through every shutoff. If the same home were in SDG&E territory, payback would drop to under 8 years.
 If your bill is the main reason you are looking, our PG&E rates guide and SCE rates guide show which plan to pair a battery with.
 How does a home battery help during a PSPS shutoff?
 A home battery keeps your critical loads running automatically when your utility cuts power for wildfire safety. Six California utilities can call a Public Safety Power Shutoff: PG&E, SCE, SDG&E, Liberty Utilities, Bear Valley Electric Service and PacifiCorp, according to the CPUC .
 A few PSPS-specific tips from our installs in fire-risk areas:
 Turn on storm watch. Most batteries can top up to 100% automatically when a red flag warning or PSPS alert hits your area, instead of sitting at your everyday reserve.
 Keep a reserve year-round. We set a 20% to 30% backup reserve so the battery is never empty when a shutoff arrives with little notice.
 Check your address. Your utility’s PSPS address lookup and the CPUC’s post-event reports show how often your area has been shut off, which is the best guide to how big your battery should be.
 Ask about Medical Baseline. If someone in your home relies on powered medical equipment, tell your utility and tell us. It changes how we size the system.
 Home battery vs generator vs portable power station
 A permanent home battery is the best choice for frequent shutoffs, silent operation and daily bill savings. A gas or propane standby generator is cheaper for very long outages but cannot save you money on normal days. A portable power station is the cheapest way to keep a fridge and phones going, but it does not switch on automatically.
 Backup power options for California homes 
 Option Typical cost Switches on automatically Lowers your bill Best for 
 Home battery (installed) $13,000 to $19,000 for one Yes Yes, on time-of-use plans Frequent PSPS events, homes with or adding solar 
 Standby generator Varies widely by size and fuel line Yes No Rural homes with multi-day outages and gas or propane on site 
 Portable power station About $1,600 to $8,000 for whole-home-capable kits in retail listings, October 2026 Only with an add-on panel Rarely Renters, short outages, a few key appliances 
 Source: home battery ranges from our California quotes; portable power station prices from retail listings checked October 28, 2026.
 Generators also come with noise rules, fuel storage and, in some California air districts, limits on how often you can run them. Our side-by-side of a solar battery vs a gas generator goes deeper.
 What does installing a home battery backup involve?
 A typical California home battery install takes one to two days on site, but the full process from signed contract to switching it on usually runs 4 to 10 weeks because of permitting and utility approval.
 Site visit or virtual survey. We look at your panel, your usage and where the battery can legally sit.
 Design and load selection. You choose critical loads or whole-home backup.
 Permit. The city or county reviews the plans; some require a fire department sign-off.
 Install. Battery, gateway and any panel work, usually in one or two days.
 Inspection and utility approval. Then we commission the system and set your backup reserve.
 Every battery we install is backed by our CA contractor license #1026168, and we handle the permit and the utility paperwork. Explore our home battery backup installation service to see how we approach it in your area, including Los Angeles County .
 Frequently asked questions
 How much does a home battery backup cost in California? About $13,000 to $19,000 installed for one battery on a critical-loads panel, and about $23,000 to $44,000 for whole-home backup with 2 to 3 batteries, as of November 2026. A panel upgrade adds about $2,500 to $5,000 when needed.
 Can I get a home battery backup without solar panels? Yes. Most modern batteries can be charged from the grid alone. The catch is that they cannot recharge during an outage, so battery-only works best for outages of a day or less.
 How long will a home battery last during a power outage? One 13.5 kWh battery runs a typical critical-loads panel (fridge, lights, Wi-Fi, furnace fan) for about 24 to 36 hours. With solar recharging it during the day, it can keep going through a multi-day shutoff.
 Is a home battery better than a generator? For most California homes with frequent but short shutoffs, yes: it is silent, automatic and lowers your bill on time-of-use rates. A generator wins for very long rural outages where you have a fuel supply.
 How many batteries do I need to run my whole house? Usually two or three, depending on your central AC and whether you have an EV or pool pump. A critical-loads setup needs one.
 Is there still a rebate for home batteries in California? The federal 25D credit ended for homeowner systems installed after December 31, 2025. SGIP equity funding of $1.10 per Wh is still available for income-qualified households, but most of it is waitlisted. Check the SGIP dashboard before you count on it.
 Get a home battery quote
 If a PSPS notice or a peak-hour bill sent you here, the fastest next step is a quote built on your actual panel and usage. Get a quote in 2 minutes , or book a virtual consultation and we will tell you honestly whether one battery, three batteries or a battery at all makes sense for your home.
